concepts.title: Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers
concepts.content_raw: Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.1)
  • LO 1.1.A: Represent patterns and algorithms found in everyday life.
  • LO 1.1.B: Explain how code is compiled and executed.
  • LO 1.1.C: Identify types of programming errors.
TermDefinition
AlgorithmA step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or performing a task.
CompilerA program that translates source code into bytecode or machine code before execution.
IDEIntegrated Development Environment — provides tools for writing, compiling, and running code.
Syntax ErrorA mistake where the rules of the programming language are not followed; caught by the compiler.
Logic ErrorCode runs but produces incorrect results; found through testing.
Run-time ErrorAn error that occurs during program execution and terminates the program abnormally.
ExceptionA specific type of run-time error that interrupts normal program flow.

Algorithms in Everyday Life (LO 1.1.A)

An algorithm is a finite set of step-by-step instructions to accomplish a task (EK 1.1.A.1). You follow algorithms every day — a recipe for baking cookies, directions to school, or the steps to tie your shoes. In computer science, we express algorithms as programs that a computer can execute.

Sequencing means the steps must be performed in a specific order (EK 1.1.A.2). Changing the order of steps can produce entirely different (often wrong) results. Consider making a sandwich: you must place ingredients between the bread, not before you get the bread out.

How Java Programs Are Compiled and Run (LO 1.1.B)

Java is a compiled language. The process works like this:

  1. You write Java source code in a .java file using an IDE (EK 1.1.B.1).
  2. The Java compiler (javac) translates source code into bytecode stored in a .class file (EK 1.1.B.2).
  3. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) executes the bytecode on any platform.

An IDE such as IntelliJ, Eclipse, or VS Code provides tools to write, compile, and run your code in one place (EK 1.1.B.1). The compiler checks your code for certain errors (syntax errors) before the program runs (EK 1.1.B.2). If the compiler finds errors, it will not produce the .class file and will display error messages.

Types of Programming Errors (LO 1.1.C)

There are three main categories of errors in Java:

1. Syntax Errors (EK 1.1.C.1): These occur when the rules of the Java language are not followed. The compiler detects these and prevents the program from compiling. Examples include missing semicolons, unmatched braces, or misspelled keywords.

// Syntax error: missing semicolon
System.out.println("Hello")
// Syntax error: misspelled keyword
pubic static void main(String[] args) { }

2. Logic Errors (EK 1.1.C.2): The program compiles and runs, but produces incorrect results. These are the hardest errors to find because the compiler cannot detect them. You discover them through testing.

// Logic error: should be (a + b) / 2 for average
double average = a + b / 2;  // missing parentheses

3. Run-time Errors (EK 1.1.C.3): These occur while the program is executing and cause it to terminate abnormally. An exception is a specific type of run-time error that interrupts the normal flow of execution (EK 1.1.C.4).

// Run-time error: division by zero
int result = 10 / 0;  // throws ArithmeticException
Worked Example 1: Identify the error type.
int x = 5;
int y = 0;
System.out.println(x / y);  // ArithmeticException

This is a run-time error (specifically an exception). The code compiles successfully but crashes when executed because you cannot divide by zero.

Worked Example 2: Identify the error type.
// Goal: print numbers 1 to 5
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i + 1);  // prints 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
}

This is a logic error. The code compiles and runs without crashing, but the output is wrong — it prints 2 through 6 instead of 1 through 5.

AP Trap: Students often confuse logic errors with run-time errors. Remember: logic errors produce wrong output but the program doesn't crash. Run-time errors cause the program to terminate abnormally.
AP Trap: An exception IS a run-time error, but not all run-time errors are exceptions. An infinite loop, for example, is a run-time error but not an exception.
Summary
  • An algorithm is a step-by-step process; sequencing is the order of steps.
  • Java source code (.java) is compiled to bytecode (.class) by javac, then run by the JVM.
  • An IDE provides tools to write, compile, and run code.
  • Syntax errors break language rules and are caught by the compiler.
  • Logic errors produce wrong results and are caught by testing.
  • Run-time errors crash the program during execution.
  • Exceptions are a type of run-time error that interrupts normal flow.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers

problems.question_html: Which type of error is detected by the Java compiler before the program runs?

hints.text: Think about which errors prevent the program from compiling.
The compiler checks that the rules of Java are followed correctly.

solution_steps.text: The compiler translates source code to bytecode. If the code violates Java's syntax rules, the compiler reports an error.
Syntax errors are detected at compile time. Logic errors are found through testing, and run-time errors occur during execution.

problems.question_html: A program compiles without errors but produces an incorrect output. What type of error does this describe?

hints.text: The program compiles — so it's not a syntax error.
The program runs but gives wrong results — it doesn't crash.

solution_steps.text: Since the program compiles, it's not a syntax error. Since it runs without crashing, it's not a run-time error.
A logic error causes incorrect behavior or output. It is detected through testing.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is an example of a run-time error?

choices.text: Missing a semicolon at the end of a statement
Using a wrong formula to compute the average
Dividing an integer by zero during execution

hints.text: Run-time errors happen while the program is running, not during compilation.
Division by zero causes an ArithmeticException at run time.

solution_steps.text: Missing semicolons and misspellings are syntax errors (caught at compile time).
A wrong formula is a logic error (wrong output, no crash).
Dividing by zero throws an ArithmeticException during execution — a run-time error.

problems.question_html: What is the role of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM)?

choices.text: It writes Java source code automatically
It translates source code into bytecode
It executes bytecode on the computer
It detects logic errors in the program

hints.text: The compiler produces bytecode. What executes it?
The JVM is what makes Java platform-independent — it runs bytecode on any OS.

solution_steps.text: The Java compiler (javac) translates source code to bytecode.
The JVM executes the bytecode, allowing the same .class file to run on any platform.

problems.question_html: Which of the following statements about exceptions is true?

choices.text: Exceptions are detected by the compiler before the program runs
Exceptions are a type of logic error
Exceptions are a type of run-time error that interrupts normal program flow
Exceptions always cause the program to produce wrong output without crashing

hints.text: Exceptions occur during program execution, not at compile time.
An exception interrupts normal flow and can terminate the program.

solution_steps.text: Exceptions are not compile-time errors — they occur during execution.
Exceptions are a specific category of run-time errors that interrupt the normal flow of the program (EK 1.1.C.4).

problems.question_html: What file extension does the Java compiler produce as output?

hints.text: The compiler converts .java files into bytecode files.
The bytecode file extension starts with a dot followed by the word for a blueprint of an object.

solution_steps.text: The Java compiler (javac) takes a .java source file as input.
It produces a .class file containing bytecode that the JVM can execute.

problems.question_html: An algorithm must have steps performed in a specific order. What is this concept called?

hints.text: Think of the word that means putting things in a sequence.
It starts with the letter 's' and relates to the order of steps.

solution_steps.text: Algorithms require steps to be performed in a defined order.
This concept is called sequencing — defining the order in which steps are executed.

concepts.title: Variables and Data Types
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.2)
  • LO 1.2.A: Identify the most appropriate data type category for a given specification.
  • LO 1.2.B: Develop code to declare variables of number and Boolean data types.
TermDefinition
Data TypeA set of values and the operations that can be performed on those values.
Primitive TypeA basic data type built into Java (e.g., int, double, boolean).
Reference TypeA data type used for objects; the variable stores a reference (memory address).
intA primitive type for whole numbers (e.g., -3, 0, 42).
doubleA primitive type for decimal numbers (e.g., 3.14, -0.5).
booleanA primitive type with only two values: true or false.
VariableA named storage location in memory that holds a value of a specific type.

Primitive vs. Reference Types (LO 1.2.A)

Every value in Java has a data type — a set of values and operations that can be performed on them (EK 1.2.A.1). Java data types fall into two categories:

Primitive types store actual values directly in memory (EK 1.2.A.2). They are used for simple numbers and Boolean values. The three primitive types on the AP exam are int, double, and boolean (EK 1.2.B.1).

Reference types are used for objects. A reference variable stores a memory address that points to the object, not the object itself (EK 1.2.A.3). Examples include String, Scanner, and any class you define.

Declaring Variables (LO 1.2.B)

A variable is a named storage location with a name and a data type (EK 1.2.B.2). You declare a variable by specifying its type followed by its name:

int age;
double gpa;
boolean isEnrolled;

You can also declare and initialize a variable in one statement:

int score = 95;
double pi = 3.14159;
boolean passed = true;

Variable names in Java are case-sensitive, must start with a letter (or underscore), and by convention use camelCase.

Worked Example 1: Choosing the right data type.

You need to store a student's test score (whole number), their GPA (decimal), and whether they passed (yes/no). What data types should you use?

int testScore = 87;
double gpa = 3.75;
boolean passed = true;

Use int for whole numbers, double for decimals, and boolean for true/false values.

Worked Example 2: Primitive vs. Reference.
int count = 10;          // primitive — stores value directly
String name = "Alice";   // reference — stores address of String object

count holds the value 10 directly. name holds a reference (memory address) pointing to the String object "Alice" in memory.

AP Trap: The AP exam only tests three primitive types: int, double, and boolean. Do NOT use long, short, byte, float, or char on the exam.
AP Trap: Java is case-sensitive. int is a data type but Int is not. Similarly, boolean is correct but Boolean refers to the wrapper class (not tested).
Summary
  • A data type defines a set of values and operations (EK 1.2.A.1).
  • Primitive types store values directly; reference types store memory addresses.
  • AP exam primitive types: int (whole numbers), double (decimals), boolean (true/false).
  • A variable is declared with a type and name: int age = 17;
  • Variable names are case-sensitive and use camelCase by convention.
  • Exclusion: long, short, byte, float, char are NOT on the AP exam.
Out of Scope: The primitive types long, short, byte, float, and char are not part of the AP CS A curriculum and will not appear on the exam.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a primitive data type in Java?

hints.text: Primitive types store simple values directly, not objects.
The three AP primitive types are int, double, and boolean.

solution_steps.text: String, Scanner, and ArrayList are all reference types (classes/objects).
double is one of the three primitive types tested on the AP exam (int, double, boolean).

problems.question_html: What is the key difference between primitive and reference types in Java?

choices.text: Primitive types can only store numbers
Reference types are faster than primitive types
Primitive types store values directly; reference types store memory addresses
Reference types cannot be used in expressions

hints.text: Think about what the variable actually holds in memory.
A primitive variable holds the value itself; a reference variable holds an address pointing to an object.

solution_steps.text: Primitive variables store the actual value (e.g., int x = 5 stores the number 5).
Reference variables store a memory address that points to an object stored elsewhere in memory.

problems.question_html: Which of the following variable declarations is valid in Java?

hints.text: Variable names cannot start with a digit or contain hyphens.
'class' is a reserved keyword in Java and cannot be used as a variable name.

solution_steps.text: 2ndPlace starts with a digit — invalid. my-score contains a hyphen — invalid. class is a reserved keyword — invalid.
boolean isValid = true; is a valid declaration with a proper camelCase name.

problems.question_html: Consider: String greeting = "Hello";. Which statement is true?

choices.text: greeting stores the characters H-e-l-l-o directly
greeting stores a reference (memory address) to the String object "Hello"
greeting cannot be changed after initialization

hints.text: String is a reference type, not a primitive type.
Reference variables store memory addresses, not the actual object data.

solution_steps.text: String is a reference type, so greeting stores a memory address pointing to the String object.
The actual characters 'Hello' are stored in the String object in memory; greeting just holds the address.

problems.question_html: What data type should be used to store the value true or false in Java?

hints.text: It's one of the three primitive types on the AP exam.
It starts with 'b' and can only hold two possible values.

solution_steps.text: In Java, true/false values are stored using the boolean data type.
boolean is a primitive type: boolean passed = true;

problems.question_html: What Java data type would you use to store the value 3.14?

hints.text: This is a decimal number, not a whole number.
The AP exam uses this type for all floating-point values (not float).

solution_steps.text: 3.14 is a decimal number, so it cannot be stored in an int.
The correct type is double, which stores floating-point (decimal) numbers.

problems.question_html:
Write Java code that declares and initializes three variables:

  • A variable named numStudents to store the whole number 30
  • A variable named averageScore to store the decimal value 89.5
  • A variable named isFull to store the value false
problems.correct_answer:
int numStudents = 30;
double averageScore = 89.5;
boolean isFull = false;
rubric: Uses int for the whole number variable
Uses double for the decimal variable
Uses boolean for the true/false variable
All variable names match the specification exactly

hints.text: Choose the correct primitive type for each kind of value.
Whole numbers use int, decimals use double, true/false uses boolean.

solution_steps.text: numStudents holds a whole number, so use int: int numStudents = 30;
averageScore holds a decimal, so use double: double averageScore = 89.5;
isFull holds true/false, so use boolean: boolean isFull = false;

concepts.title: Expressions and Output
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.3)
  • LO 1.3.A: Develop code for output using System.out.print and System.out.println and determine the result displayed.
  • LO 1.3.B: Develop code using string literals and determine the result.
  • LO 1.3.C: Develop code using arithmetic expressions and determine the result.
TermDefinition
System.out.printDisplays text without moving to a new line afterward.
System.out.printlnDisplays text and then moves to a new line.
String literalA sequence of characters enclosed in double quotes.
Escape sequenceA backslash followed by a character that represents a special character (e.g., \n, \", \\).
Operator precedenceRules that determine the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression.
ArithmeticExceptionA run-time error thrown when dividing an integer by zero.

Output with print and println (LO 1.3.A)

System.out.print and System.out.println display information to the console (EK 1.3.A.1). The key difference is that println adds a newline at the end, while print does not.

System.out.print("Hello ");   // cursor stays on same line
System.out.println("World");  // prints "World" then moves to next line
System.out.println("!");      // prints "!" on a new line

Output:

Hello World
!

String Literals and Escape Sequences (LO 1.3.B)

A literal is a fixed value written directly in your code (EK 1.3.B.1). A string literal is a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotes, like "Hello" (EK 1.3.B.2).

Escape sequences represent special characters inside strings (EK 1.3.B.3):

  • \\ — backslash character (\)
  • \" — double quote character (")
  • \n — newline (moves to next line)
System.out.println("She said \"Hi\"");  // She said "Hi"
System.out.println("Line1\nLine2");      // Line1  (then new line)  Line2
System.out.println("Path: C:\\Users");    // Path: C:\Users

Arithmetic Expressions (LO 1.3.C)

Java supports five arithmetic operators (EK 1.3.C.1):

  • + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication
  • / division, % remainder (modulo)

Integer division (EK 1.3.C.2): When both operands are int, division truncates the decimal part (no rounding). 7 / 2 evaluates to 3, not 3.5.

Double division (EK 1.3.C.3): If either operand is a double, the result is a double. 7.0 / 2 evaluates to 3.5.

Remainder operator % (EK 1.3.C.4): Returns the remainder after division. 7 % 3 is 1 because 7 = 3 * 2 + 1.

Operator precedence (EK 1.3.C.5): *, /, % are evaluated before + and -. Use parentheses to change the order.

int result = 2 + 3 * 4;    // 14 (not 20)
int result2 = (2 + 3) * 4;  // 20

ArithmeticException (EK 1.3.C.6): Dividing an integer by zero throws an ArithmeticException at run time. Note: dividing a double by zero does NOT throw an exception — it produces Infinity or NaN.

Worked Example 1: Trace the output.
System.out.print("AP ");
System.out.print("CS ");
System.out.println("A");
System.out.println("Java");

Output:
AP CS A
Java
The first two print calls stay on the same line. println("A") finishes the first line. println("Java") prints on the next line.

Worked Example 2: Integer vs. double division.
System.out.println(17 / 5);    // 3
System.out.println(17.0 / 5);  // 3.4
System.out.println(17 % 5);    // 2

17 / 5 = 3 (integer division truncates). 17.0 / 5 = 3.4 (double division). 17 % 5 = 2 (remainder).

AP Trap: Integer division truncates — it does NOT round. 7 / 4 is 1, not 2. It simply drops the decimal part.
AP Trap: System.out.print vs System.out.println — forgetting the difference between these is a common source of wrong answers on code-tracing questions.
Summary
  • System.out.print outputs text; println outputs text + newline.
  • String literals use double quotes. Escape sequences: \\, \", \n.
  • Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 = 3.
  • If either operand is double, the result is double: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5.
  • % gives the remainder: 7 % 3 = 1.
  • *, /, % are evaluated before +, -.
  • Dividing an integer by zero throws ArithmeticException.

problems.question_html:
What is the output of the following code?

System.out.print("Hello");
System.out.println(" World");
System.out.println("!");

hints.text: print does not add a newline; println does.
After print("Hello"), the cursor stays on the same line. println(" World") adds " World" then moves to the next line.

solution_steps.text: print("Hello") outputs "Hello" with cursor at end. println(" World") appends " World" then newline.
println("!") prints "!" on the next line. Final output: "Hello World" on line 1, "!" on line 2.

problems.question_html: What is the value of the expression 2 + 3 * 4 - 1?

hints.text: Remember operator precedence: multiplication before addition/subtraction.

solution_steps.text: By operator precedence, * is evaluated first: 3 * 4 = 12.
Then left to right: 2 + 12 = 14, then 14 - 1 = 13.

problems.question_html:
What does the following code print?

System.out.println("She said \"Hi\"");

hints.text: The \" escape sequence represents a literal double quote character.
Each \" in the string becomes a single " in the output.

solution_steps.text: The escape sequence \" produces a literal double-quote character in the output.
So the output is: She said "Hi"

problems.question_html:
What is the output of the following expression?

System.out.println(13 / 5);

hints.text: Both operands are integers, so integer division is used.
Integer division truncates the decimal part. 13 / 5 = 2.6, truncated to 2.

solution_steps.text: Both 13 and 5 are int values, so Java performs integer division.
13 / 5 = 2 (the .6 is truncated, not rounded). Output: 2

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println(17 % 5);

hints.text: % is the remainder operator.
17 divided by 5 is 3 remainder 2.

solution_steps.text: 17 % 5 computes the remainder when 17 is divided by 5.
17 = 5 * 3 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println(7.0 / 2);

hints.text: One operand is a double (7.0). What happens?
If either operand is double, the result is double: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5.

solution_steps.text: 7.0 is a double, so Java performs double division.
7.0 / 2 = 3.5. The output is 3.5.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println(3 + 4 * 2 - 8 / 4);

hints.text: Apply operator precedence: * and / before + and -.

solution_steps.text: Evaluate * and / first (left to right): 4 * 2 = 8, 8 / 4 = 2.
Then + and - left to right: 3 + 8 - 2 = 9.

problems.question_html:
Write a complete Java statement that prints the following output exactly (including the newline in the middle):

Hello "World"
Goodbye
rubric: Uses System.out.println or appropriate print statements
Correctly uses \" for the double quotes around World
Correctly uses \n for the newline between the two lines

hints.text: You need escape sequences for the quotes and the newline.
Use \" for double quotes and \n for the newline character.

solution_steps.text: To print a literal double quote, use the escape sequence \"
To print a newline within a string, use \n.
Combined: System.out.println("Hello \"World\"\nGoodbye");

concepts.title: Assignment Statements and Input
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.4)
  • LO 1.4.A: Develop code using assignment statements with expressions.
  • LO 1.4.B: Read input from the user.
TermDefinition
Assignment operator (=)Stores the value of the right-hand expression into the left-hand variable.
InitializationThe first time a variable is given a value.
ExpressionA combination of values, variables, and operators that evaluates to a single value.
ScannerA class in java.util used to read input from the keyboard.

Assignment Statements (LO 1.4.A)

An assignment statement stores a value into a variable using the = operator. The right side is evaluated first, then the result is stored in the variable on the left side (EK 1.4.A.2).

When a variable receives its first value, this is called initialization (EK 1.4.A.1). Attempting to use a variable before it is initialized causes a compile-time error.

int x = 5;          // declaration + initialization
int y;               // declaration only
y = x + 3;           // assignment: y gets 8
x = x + 1;           // x is now 6 (evaluate right side first)

The expression on the right side is fully evaluated before the assignment occurs (EK 1.4.A.3). This means x = x + 1 works: Java evaluates x + 1 (= 6), then stores 6 back into x.

Reading Input with Scanner (LO 1.4.B)

The Scanner class allows your program to read input from the keyboard (EK 1.4.B.1):

import java.util.Scanner;

Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
System.out.print("Enter your age: ");
int age = input.nextInt();
System.out.print("Enter your GPA: ");
double gpa = input.nextDouble();

Common Scanner methods: nextInt(), nextDouble(), next() (reads one word), and nextLine() (reads entire line).

Worked Example 1: Tracing assignment statements.
int a = 10;
int b = 3;
a = a + b;   // a is now 13
b = a - b;   // b is now 10
System.out.println(a + " " + b);  // 13 10

Trace: Initially a=10, b=3. After a = a + b: a=13, b=3. After b = a - b: a=13, b=10. Output: 13 10

Worked Example 2: Common pattern — swapping values.
int x = 5, y = 9;
int temp = x;  // temp = 5
x = y;         // x = 9
y = temp;      // y = 5
System.out.println(x + " " + y);  // 9 5

You need a temporary variable to swap — direct assignment like x = y; y = x; would lose the original value of x.

AP Trap: The = operator is NOT equality — it is assignment. It means "store the right side into the left side." Equality is tested with ==.
AP Trap: x = x + 1; is valid. The right side is evaluated first using the current value of x, then the result is stored back into x.
Summary
  • The assignment operator = stores the right-side value into the left-side variable.
  • The right side is fully evaluated before assignment occurs.
  • Initialization is the first assignment to a variable.
  • Using a variable before initialization causes a compile error.
  • Scanner reads keyboard input with methods like nextInt() and nextDouble().
  • Swapping two variables requires a temporary variable.
Out of Scope: The specific form of user input (i.e., how the Scanner reads input behind the scenes) is not tested on the AP exam.

problems.question_html:
What is the value of b after these statements execute?

int a = 5;
int b = 10;
a = b;
b = a;

hints.text: After a = b, what is the value of a?
After a = b, a becomes 10. Then b = a assigns 10 to b. Both are 10.

solution_steps.text: Initially: a = 5, b = 10.
a = b: a becomes 10 (b is still 10).
b = a: b becomes 10 (a is 10). Final b = 10.

problems.question_html: Which of the following correctly reads an integer from the keyboard using Scanner?

hints.text: Scanner methods are called on a Scanner object, not on the class name.
Assuming 'input' is a Scanner object, you call input.nextInt().

solution_steps.text: Scanner methods are instance methods — called on a Scanner object (e.g., input).
input.nextInt() reads and returns the next integer from keyboard input.

problems.question_html: What happens if you try to use a variable that has been declared but not initialized?

choices.text: The variable automatically gets the value 0
The program compiles but throws a run-time error
The variable gets the value null

hints.text: Java requires local variables to be initialized before use.
The compiler checks for this and refuses to compile if a variable might be uninitialized.

solution_steps.text: In Java, local variables must be initialized before they are used.
If a local variable might not be initialized, the compiler reports a compile-time error.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

int x = 7;
x = x + 3;
System.out.println(x);

hints.text: Evaluate the right side first: x + 3 = 7 + 3.
x + 3 = 10, which is then stored back into x.

solution_steps.text: x starts at 7. The expression x + 3 evaluates to 10.
10 is stored into x. System.out.println(x) prints 10.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

int a = 4;
int b = 7;
int temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;
System.out.println(a + " " + b);

hints.text: This is a swap pattern. Trace each assignment step by step.
temp saves a's original value (4). a gets b's value (7). b gets temp (4).

solution_steps.text: Initially: a=4, b=7. temp=a: temp=4.
a=b: a=7. b=temp: b=4. Output: 7 4

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

int x = 3;
int y = x * 2 + 1;
x = y - x;
System.out.println(x + " " + y);

hints.text: Evaluate each assignment step by step. What is y after x * 2 + 1?

solution_steps.text: x = y - x = 7 - 3 = 4. Output: 4 7

problems.question_html:
Write Java code that:

  1. Declares an int variable a initialized to 8
  2. Declares an int variable b initialized to 3
  3. Stores the sum of a and b into a new variable sum

concepts.title: Casting and Range of Variables
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.5)
  • LO 1.5.A: Evaluate expressions that cast primitive values.
  • LO 1.5.B: Explain the conditions that lead to integer overflow.
  • LO 1.5.C: Explain the limitations to the accuracy of double values.
TermDefinition
CastingExplicitly converting a value from one data type to another.
TruncationRemoving the decimal part when casting a double to an int (no rounding).
WideningAutomatic conversion from a smaller type (int) to a larger type (double).
NarrowingExplicit conversion from a larger type (double) to a smaller type (int); requires a cast.
Integer.MAX_VALUEThe largest int value: 2,147,483,647.
OverflowWhen a computation exceeds the range of a data type, wrapping to an unexpected value.
Round-off errorSmall inaccuracies that occur because doubles cannot represent all decimal values exactly.

Casting Primitive Values (LO 1.5.A)

Casting converts a value from one type to another. Place the target type in parentheses before the value:

double d = 7.9;
int n = (int) d;     // n = 7 (truncation, NOT rounding)
int x = 5;
double y = (double) x;  // y = 5.0

Casting to int truncates — it removes the decimal portion without rounding (EK 1.5.A.1, EK 1.5.A.2).

Widening (int to double) happens automatically and never loses information (EK 1.5.A.3):

int a = 10;
double b = a;  // automatic widening: b = 10.0

Rounding formula (EK 1.5.A.4): To round a positive double to the nearest int:

int rounded = (int)(d + 0.5);  // rounds 7.9 to 8, 7.4 to 7

Casting in Arithmetic

A common use of casting is to get double division from int values:

int a = 7, b = 2;
double result = (double) a / b;  // 3.5 (a is cast to 7.0 first)
double wrong  = (double)(a / b); // 3.0 (integer division happens first!)

The cast applies only to the value immediately following it. (double) a / b casts a to 7.0, then divides 7.0 / 2 = 3.5. But (double)(a / b) does integer division first (7/2 = 3), then casts 3 to 3.0.

Integer Overflow (LO 1.5.B)

The int type can hold values from Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2,147,483,648) to Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647) (EK 1.5.B.1, EK 1.5.B.2). If a computation exceeds this range, overflow occurs and the value wraps around to an unexpected number (EK 1.5.B.3).

int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE;  // 2147483647
int overflow = big + 1;       // -2147483648 (wraps around!)

Round-off Errors with Doubles (LO 1.5.C)

Doubles use binary floating-point representation and cannot store all decimal values exactly (EK 1.5.C.1). This leads to tiny inaccuracies called round-off errors:

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);  // 0.30000000000000004 (not 0.3!)
Worked Example 1: Casting for accurate division.
int total = 17;
int count = 5;
double avg = (double) total / count;
System.out.println(avg);  // 3.4

Without the cast, 17 / 5 = 3 (integer division). The cast converts total to 17.0 first, so 17.0 / 5 = 3.4.

Worked Example 2: Rounding.
double grade = 89.6;
int rounded = (int)(grade + 0.5);  // (int)(90.1) = 90
System.out.println(rounded);  // 90
AP Trap: (double)(a / b) is NOT the same as (double) a / b. The first does integer division first, then casts. The second casts a first, then does double division.
AP Trap: Casting to int TRUNCATES — it does not round. (int) 9.99 is 9, not 10.
Summary
  • (int) casts a double to int by truncation (drops decimal, no rounding).
  • (double) casts int to double; widening also happens automatically.
  • Rounding formula: (int)(value + 0.5) for positive numbers.
  • Integer.MAX_VALUE = 2,147,483,647; adding 1 causes overflow.
  • Doubles have round-off errors because binary cannot represent all decimals exactly.
  • Cast placement matters: (double) a / b ≠ (double)(a / b).

concepts.title: Compound Assignment Operators
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.6)
  • LO 1.6.A: Develop code using compound assignment operators.
TermDefinition
+=Adds right operand to variable and stores result: x += 3 means x = x + 3.
-=Subtracts right operand: x -= 2 means x = x - 2.
*=Multiplies: x *= 4 means x = x * 4.
/=Divides: x /= 2 means x = x / 2.
%=Remainder: x %= 3 means x = x % 3.
++Post-increment: x++ means x = x + 1.
--Post-decrement: x-- means x = x - 1.

Compound Assignment Operators (LO 1.6.A)

Compound assignment operators combine an arithmetic operation with assignment (EK 1.6.A.1). They are shorthand for common update patterns:

int x = 10;
x += 5;   // x = x + 5 → x is 15
x -= 3;   // x = x - 3 → x is 12
x *= 2;   // x = x * 2 → x is 24
x /= 4;   // x = x / 4 → x is 6
x %= 4;   // x = x % 4 → x is 2

Increment and Decrement (EK 1.6.A.2)

The post-increment operator ++ adds 1, and post-decrement -- subtracts 1:

int count = 5;
count++;   // count is now 6 (same as count = count + 1)
count--;   // count is now 5 (same as count = count - 1)

On the AP exam, ++ and -- are used only as standalone statements, not inside larger expressions. The prefix forms (++x, --x) are not tested.

Worked Example 1: Tracing compound operators.
int a = 20;
a -= 8;    // a = 20 - 8 = 12
a *= 3;    // a = 12 * 3 = 36
a /= 9;    // a = 36 / 9 = 4
a++;       // a = 4 + 1 = 5
System.out.println(a);  // 5
Worked Example 2: Using %= to check divisibility.
int num = 17;
num %= 5;   // num = 17 % 5 = 2
System.out.println(num);  // 2

The %= operator stores the remainder. Useful for cycling through ranges.

AP Trap: The AP exam only uses x++ and x-- as standalone statements. Expressions like y = x++ (where increment is inside a larger expression) are NOT tested. The prefix forms ++x and --x are also excluded.
AP Trap: Remember that /= with integers still does integer division. int x = 7; x /= 2; results in x = 3 (not 3.5).
Summary
  • +=, -=, *=, /=, %= combine arithmetic with assignment.
  • x += n is shorthand for x = x + n (same pattern for all five).
  • x++ increments by 1; x-- decrements by 1.
  • On the AP exam, ++ and -- are standalone statements only.
  • /= with ints uses integer division (truncates).
  • Exclusion: Prefix forms (++x, --x) and ++ / -- inside expressions.

concepts.title: Application Program Interface (API) and Libraries
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.7)
  • LO 1.7.A: Identify the attributes and behaviors of an object from its API documentation.
TermDefinition
APIApplication Program Interface — a specification describing how to use a library's classes and methods.
LibraryA collection of pre-written classes and methods available for use.
PackageA group of related classes organized together (e.g., java.util).
AttributeData stored in an object (its variables/fields).
BehaviorAn action an object can perform (its methods).

What is an API? (LO 1.7.A)

An API (Application Program Interface) describes how to use a library's classes and methods without needing to understand their internal implementation (EK 1.7.A.1). Java's standard library provides thousands of pre-written classes organized into packages.

Key packages for AP CS A:

  • java.lang — automatically imported (includes String, Math, System, Object)
  • java.util — must be imported (includes Scanner, ArrayList, Arrays)

To use a class from a non-lang package, you must import it:

import java.util.Scanner;  // import specific class
import java.util.*;        // import all classes from package

Attributes vs. Behaviors (EK 1.7.A.2)

When reading API documentation, you'll see two categories of information about a class:

  • Attributes (data/variables): What the object knows or stores. For example, a Rectangle object has attributes like width and height.
  • Behaviors (methods): What the object can do. For example, a Rectangle object might have methods like getArea() and getPerimeter().

Thinking of a real-world object like a Dog: attributes include name, breed, and weight; behaviors include bark(), eat(), and sleep().

Worked Example 1: Reading an API.

Consider a BankAccount class. Its API might list:

  • Attributes: balance (double), accountNumber (String)
  • Behaviors: deposit(double amount), withdraw(double amount), getBalance()

You can use these methods without knowing how they are implemented inside the class.

Worked Example 2: Importing a library.
import java.util.Scanner;

public class InputDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter a number: ");
        int num = sc.nextInt();
    }
}

Scanner is in java.util, so it must be imported. Classes in java.lang (like String, Math) are imported automatically.

AP Trap: java.lang classes (String, Math, System) do NOT need an import statement. All other packages (like java.util) DO require an explicit import.
Summary
  • An API specifies how to use a library — what classes and methods are available.
  • A library is a collection of pre-written classes; a package groups related classes.
  • Attributes = data (variables); behaviors = actions (methods).
  • java.lang is auto-imported; other packages need import statements.
  • You can use a class's methods without knowing the internal implementation.

color and speed are attributes; getColor() and setSpeed() are behaviors

concepts.title: Documentation with Comments
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.8)
  • LO 1.8.A: Describe the functionality and use of program code through comments.
TermDefinition
// commentSingle-line comment — everything after // on that line is ignored.
/* comment */Multi-line (block) comment — everything between /* and */ is ignored.
/** comment */Javadoc comment — used to generate documentation for classes and methods.
PreconditionA condition that must be true before a method is called for it to work correctly.
PostconditionA condition that is guaranteed to be true after a method has finished executing.

Types of Comments (EK 1.8.A.1)

Java supports three types of comments, which are ignored by the compiler:

// This is a single-line comment

/* This is a
   multi-line comment */

/**
 * This is a Javadoc comment.
 * Used to document classes and methods.
 * @param name description of the parameter
 * @return description of the return value
 */

Single-line comments (//) are used for brief notes. Multi-line comments (/* */) span multiple lines. Javadoc comments (/** */) are used to generate official API documentation.

Preconditions (EK 1.8.A.2)

A precondition is a condition that the caller must ensure is true before calling a method. If the precondition is not met, the method is not guaranteed to work correctly.

/**
 * Returns the square root of a number.
 * @param n the number (precondition: n >= 0)
 * @return the square root of n
 */
public static double sqrt(double n) { ... }

The precondition n >= 0 means the caller is responsible for passing a non-negative number.

Postconditions (EK 1.8.A.3)

A postcondition describes what is guaranteed to be true after a method completes. It is the method's promise to the caller.

/**
 * Deposits money into the account.
 * @param amount the deposit amount (precondition: amount > 0)
 * postcondition: balance is increased by amount
 */
public void deposit(double amount) { ... }
Worked Example 1: Reading preconditions and postconditions.
/**
 * Returns the average of two test scores.
 * @param score1 first score (precondition: 0 <= score1 <= 100)
 * @param score2 second score (precondition: 0 <= score2 <= 100)
 * @return the average of score1 and score2
 * postcondition: return value is between 0.0 and 100.0
 */
public static double average(int score1, int score2)

The preconditions tell the caller: both scores must be 0-100. The postcondition promises the result will also be 0.0-100.0.

Worked Example 2: Comments don't affect output.
int x = 5;  // set x to 5
/* x = 10; */  // this line is commented out!
System.out.println(x);  // prints 5, not 10

The line x = 10; is inside a block comment, so it is ignored. x remains 5.

AP Trap: Comments are completely ignored by the compiler — they do not affect program behavior. Code tracing questions sometimes include commented-out lines to test if you notice them.
Summary
  • Three comment types: // (single-line), /* */ (multi-line), /** */ (Javadoc).
  • Comments are ignored by the compiler and do not affect execution.
  • Preconditions specify what must be true before a method is called.
  • Postconditions specify what is guaranteed after a method finishes.
  • The caller is responsible for meeting preconditions; the method is responsible for meeting postconditions.

a = a * 2; */

concepts.title: Method Signatures
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.9)
  • LO 1.9.A: Identify the correct method to use based on its documentation.
  • LO 1.9.B: Describe how to call methods with and without parameters.
TermDefinition
MethodA named block of code that performs a specific task and may return a value.
Method signatureThe method name plus the ordered list of parameter types.
ParameterA variable declared in the method signature that receives a value when the method is called.
ArgumentThe actual value passed to a method when it is called.
Return typeThe data type of the value a method sends back; void means no value is returned.
Overloaded methodsMultiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists.

Methods and Parameters (LO 1.9.A)

A method is a named block of code that performs a task (EK 1.9.A.1). A method can take parameters — variables that receive input values when the method is called.

The method signature consists of the method name and the parameter types in order (EK 1.9.A.2). The return type is NOT part of the signature.

// Method signature: add(int, int)
public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

Calling Methods (LO 1.9.B)

Void methods perform an action but do not return a value (EK 1.9.B.1):

System.out.println("Hello");  // void — no return value

Non-void methods return a value that can be stored or used in an expression (EK 1.9.B.2):

int result = Math.abs(-5);    // returns 5
double root = Math.sqrt(16); // returns 4.0

When calling a method, the values you pass are called arguments (EK 1.9.B.3). Arguments must match the parameter types in order.

Overloaded Methods (EK 1.9.B.4)

Overloaded methods share the same name but have different parameter lists. Java uses the number and types of arguments to determine which version to call:

// Two overloaded methods:
public static int max(int a, int b) { ... }
public static double max(double a, double b) { ... }

max(3, 7);     // calls max(int, int)
max(2.5, 1.8); // calls max(double, double)

Method Calls and Execution Flow (EK 1.9.B.5)

When a method is called, the current code pauses, the method executes, and then control returns to where the call was made. This interrupts the sequential flow of execution.

Worked Example 1: Distinguishing parameters and arguments.
public static int multiply(int x, int y) {  // x, y are parameters
    return x * y;
}

int result = multiply(4, 5);  // 4 and 5 are arguments

x and y are parameters (in the definition). 4 and 5 are arguments (in the call).

Worked Example 2: Choosing the right overloaded method.

Given: Math.abs(int) and Math.abs(double)

int a = Math.abs(-7);     // calls abs(int), returns 7
double b = Math.abs(-3.5); // calls abs(double), returns 3.5
AP Trap: Parameters are in the definition; arguments are in the call. Don't mix up these terms — the AP exam distinguishes between them.
AP Trap: The return type is NOT part of the method signature. Two methods cannot differ only by return type — they must have different parameter lists to be overloaded.
Summary
  • A method signature = method name + parameter types (in order).
  • Parameters are in the definition; arguments are in the call.
  • Void methods don't return a value; non-void methods do.
  • Overloaded methods have the same name but different parameter lists.
  • A method call interrupts sequential execution; control returns after the method finishes.
  • The return type is NOT part of the method signature.

problems.question_html:
What is the method signature of this method?

public static double average(int a, int b, int c) {
    return (a + b + c) / 3.0;
}

The signature is: average(int, int, int). Return type and access modifiers are not part of it.

solution_steps.text: A method signature consists of the method name and the ordered list of parameter types.
The return type (double) and modifiers (public static) are NOT part of the signature.
The signature is: average(int, int, int).

problems.question_html: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

A parameter is the variable in the method definition; an argument is the value passed when calling
Parameters are used in void methods; arguments in non-void methods

hints.text: One is in the definition, the other in the call.
Parameters are defined in the method header. Arguments are the actual values you pass.

solution_steps.text: Parameters appear in the method definition: public void foo(int x) — x is a parameter.
Arguments are the actual values passed when calling: foo(5) — 5 is an argument.

problems.question_html:

problems.question_html: Which statement correctly uses the return value of a non-void method?

Store the return value in a variable of the matching type.

solution_steps.text: Math.sqrt returns a double, so the return value should be stored in a double variable.

problems.question_html: A method that does not return a value has what return type?

hints.text: This keyword means 'nothing' or 'empty'.
It is a 4-letter word starting with 'v'.

solution_steps.text: In Java, methods that perform an action without returning a value are declared with the return type void.
Example: public void printName(String n) { ... }

problems.question_html: What is the term for methods that have the same name but different parameter lists?

hints.text: This is a common OOP concept where multiple methods share a name.
The word starts with 'over' and relates to having multiple versions.

solution_steps.text: When multiple methods share the same name but differ in their parameter lists, they are called overloaded methods.
Java determines which version to call based on the arguments provided.

problems.question_html:

problems.correct_answer: public static double calculateTotal(int quantity, int pricePerItem)

Method name is calculateTotal
Takes two int parameters with correct names

public static double calculateTotal(int quantity, int pricePerItem)

concepts.title: Calling Class Methods
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.10)
  • LO 1.10.A: Call class (static) methods and determine the result.
TermDefinition
Class methodA method declared with the static keyword; called on the class, not on an object.
staticA keyword indicating the method belongs to the class, not to instances of the class.
Dot operator (.)Used to access a method on a class or object: ClassName.method().
Math classA class in java.lang providing static methods for common math operations.

Static (Class) Methods (LO 1.10.A)

A class method (also called a static method) is declared with the static keyword (EK 1.10.A.1). Unlike instance methods, you do NOT need to create an object to call a static method.

Static methods are called using the class name and the dot operator (EK 1.10.A.2):

// Syntax: ClassName.methodName(arguments)
int absolute = Math.abs(-10);     // 10
double power = Math.pow(2, 3);    // 8.0
double root = Math.sqrt(25);      // 5.0

Notice the pattern: you call the method on the class (Math), not on an object. This is because the method is static — it belongs to the class itself.

When to Use Class Methods

Class methods are used when the method does not depend on any particular object's data. For example, Math.sqrt(25) computes a square root — it doesn't need a Math object because it just performs a calculation.

// Compare:
Math.abs(-5);           // class method — called on the class
str.length();            // instance method — called on an object (str)

// You CANNOT do:
// Math m = new Math();  // Math has no public constructor
// m.abs(-5);            // Not how you call static methods
Worked Example 1: Calling static methods.
int a = Math.abs(-7);          // 7
double b = Math.pow(3, 2);     // 9.0
int c = Math.max(a, (int) b);  // Math.max(7, 9) = 9
System.out.println(c);         // 9
Worked Example 2: Static method in your own class.
public class MathHelper {
    public static int square(int n) {
        return n * n;
    }
}

// Calling it:
int s = MathHelper.square(5);  // 25
AP Trap: Do not try to call a static method on an object. Use the class name: Math.abs(-5), NOT myMath.abs(-5).
Summary
  • Class (static) methods are declared with the static keyword.
  • Called using ClassName.methodName(arguments) — no object needed.
  • The dot operator (.) connects the class name to the method.
  • Examples: Math.abs(), Math.pow(), Math.sqrt().
  • Static methods belong to the class, not to any particular object.

problems.question_html: How do you correctly call a static method in Java?

hints.text: Static methods are called on the class, not on an object.
The syntax is: ClassName.methodName(arguments).

solution_steps.text: Static methods belong to the class, not to instances.
They are called using the class name and dot operator: ClassName.methodName().

problems.question_html: What keyword indicates that a method is a class method?

hints.text: This keyword means the method belongs to the class, not to objects.
It's the same keyword used in 'public static void main'.

solution_steps.text: The static keyword indicates a method belongs to the class itself.
Static methods can be called without creating an object: ClassName.method().

problems.question_html: Why can't you write Math m = new Math(); m.abs(-5);?

choices.text: Math is not a real class
Math's constructor is private; its methods are static and should be called on the class
You need to import Math first

hints.text: Math methods are static — they are called on the class name.
The Math class does not allow you to create instances; use Math.abs(-5) instead.

solution_steps.text: The Math class has a private constructor — you cannot create Math objects.
All Math methods are static and are called using Math.methodName().

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println(Math.abs(-15));

hints.text: Math.abs returns the absolute value of the argument.
The absolute value of -15 is 15.

solution_steps.text: Math.abs(-15) returns the absolute value: 15.
Output: 15.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 4));

2^4 = 16. Math.pow returns a double.

solution_steps.text: Math.pow(2, 4) computes 2 raised to the 4th power = 16.
Math.pow always returns a double, so the output is 16.0.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

int x = Math.abs(-3) + (int) Math.pow(2, 3);
System.out.println(x);

hints.text: Evaluate each method call separately, then add.
Math.abs(-3) = 3. Math.pow(2,3) = 8.0, cast to 8. Total: 11.

concepts.title: Math Class
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.11)
  • LO 1.11.A: Write expressions using Math library methods and evaluate their results.
TermDefinition
Math.abs(int)Returns the absolute value of an int.
Math.abs(double)Returns the absolute value of a double.
Math.pow(double, double)Returns the first argument raised to the power of the second. Returns double.
Math.sqrt(double)Returns the square root of the argument. Returns double.
Math.random()Returns a random double value in the range [0.0, 1.0).

Math Class Methods (LO 1.11.A)

The Math class is in java.lang, so no import is needed (EK 1.11.A.1). All Math methods are static — call them using Math.methodName().

Absolute Value — Math.abs (EK 1.11.A.2)

Math.abs(-7)    // returns 7 (int)
Math.abs(7)     // returns 7 (int)
Math.abs(-3.5)  // returns 3.5 (double)

Power — Math.pow (EK 1.11.A.2)

Math.pow(2, 10)   // returns 1024.0
Math.pow(3, 0.5)  // returns ~1.732 (square root of 3)
Math.pow(5, 0)    // returns 1.0

Math.pow always returns a double, even if both arguments are integers.

Square Root — Math.sqrt (EK 1.11.A.2)

Math.sqrt(25)   // returns 5.0
Math.sqrt(2)    // returns ~1.414

Random Numbers — Math.random (EK 1.11.A.3)

Math.random() returns a double in the range [0.0, 1.0) — includes 0.0 but excludes 1.0.

To generate random integers in a range [min, max]:

// Random int from 0 to n-1:
int r = (int)(Math.random() * n);

// Random int from min to max (inclusive):
int r = (int)(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;

// Example: random int from 1 to 6 (dice roll):
int die = (int)(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
Worked Example 1: Computing distance.
// Distance between points (3, 4) and (0, 0)
double dist = Math.sqrt(Math.pow(3, 2) + Math.pow(4, 2));
System.out.println(dist);  // 5.0

Math.pow(3, 2) = 9.0, Math.pow(4, 2) = 16.0. Math.sqrt(25.0) = 5.0.

Worked Example 2: Random number range.
// Random int from 10 to 20 (inclusive)
int r = (int)(Math.random() * 11) + 10;
// Math.random() * 11 gives [0.0, 11.0)
// (int) truncates to 0-10
// + 10 shifts to 10-20
Worked Example 3: Nesting Math calls.
int result = Math.abs(Math.min(-8, -3));
// Math.min(-8, -3) = -8
// Math.abs(-8) = 8
System.out.println(result);  // 8
AP Trap: Math.random() returns a value in [0.0, 1.0) — it can be exactly 0.0 but is NEVER exactly 1.0. Be careful with range calculations.
AP Trap: Math.pow always returns a double. If you need an int result, you must cast: (int) Math.pow(2, 3) gives 8.
Summary
  • Math class is in java.lang — no import needed. All methods are static.
  • Math.abs(x) — absolute value (int or double).
  • Math.pow(base, exp) — power, always returns double.
  • Math.sqrt(x) — square root, returns double.
  • Math.random() — random double in [0.0, 1.0).
  • Range formula: (int)(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min.
  • Always cast Math.pow/Math.sqrt results if you need an int.

problems.question_html: What is the range of values returned by Math.random()?

hints.text: Math.random() can be exactly 0.0 but never exactly 1.0.
The range uses square bracket for 0.0 (inclusive) and parenthesis for 1.0 (exclusive).

solution_steps.text: Math.random() generates a double d where 0.0 <= d < 1.0.
This is written as [0.0, 1.0) — includes 0.0, excludes 1.0.

problems.question_html: Which expression generates a random integer from 1 to 10 (inclusive)?

hints.text: The formula is (int)(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min.
For 1 to 10: (int)(Math.random() * 10) gives 0-9, then + 1 gives 1-10.

solution_steps.text: Math.random() * 10 gives [0.0, 10.0). (int) truncates to 0-9.
Adding 1 shifts the range to 1-10. Answer: (int)(Math.random() * 10) + 1.

problems.question_html: Which expression generates a random integer from 5 to 15 (inclusive)?

hints.text: Use the formula: (int)(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min.
max - min + 1 = 15 - 5 + 1 = 11. So: (int)(Math.random() * 11) + 5.

solution_steps.text: Range: 5 to 15 inclusive. Number of values: 15 - 5 + 1 = 11.
(int)(Math.random() * 11) gives 0-10. Adding 5 gives 5-15.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

solution_steps.text: Math.sqrt(81) computes the square root of 81 = 9.
Math.sqrt returns a double, so the output is 9.0.

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

System.out.println((int) Math.pow(3, 3));

hints.text: Math.pow(3, 3) computes 3 cubed.
3^3 = 27.0, cast to int gives 27.

solution_steps.text: Math.pow(3, 3) = 27.0 (returns double).

problems.question_html:
What is the output?

double d = Math.sqrt(Math.pow(3, 2) + Math.pow(4, 2));

problems.question_html: Write a Java expression that computes the distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) using the distance formula: d = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). Store the result in a double variable called distance. Assume x1, y1, x2, y2 are already declared as doubles.
problems.correct_answer: double distance = Math.sqrt(Math.pow(x2 - x1, 2) + Math.pow(y2 - y1, 2));
rubric: Uses Math.sqrt for the outer square root
Uses Math.pow for each squared difference
Correctly subtracts coordinates (x2-x1) and (y2-y1)
Stores result in a double variable named distance

hints.text: Use Math.pow(value, 2) to square a value and Math.sqrt() for the square root.
The structure is: Math.sqrt(Math.pow(x2-x1, 2) + Math.pow(y2-y1, 2))

solution_steps.text: Square the differences: Math.pow(x2 - x1, 2) and Math.pow(y2 - y1, 2).
Add them and take the square root: Math.sqrt(sum).

concepts.title: Objects: Instances of Classes
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.12)
  • LO 1.12.A: Explain the relationship between a class and an object.
  • LO 1.12.B: Declare reference type variables.
TermDefinition
ClassA blueprint or template that defines the attributes and behaviors of objects.
ObjectA specific instance of a class with its own set of attribute values.
InstanceAnother term for an object — a specific realization of a class.
Reference variableA variable that stores a memory address pointing to an object.
Object classThe root of Java's class hierarchy — all classes extend Object.

Classes and Objects (LO 1.12.A)

A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines what attributes (data) and behaviors (methods) all objects of that type will have (EK 1.12.A.1). An object is a specific instance of a class, with its own values for the attributes defined by the class (EK 1.12.A.2).

Think of it like this: the class Dog defines that all dogs have a name, breed, and age. A specific dog object might have name="Buddy", breed="Labrador", age=3.

Java has a class hierarchy — all classes ultimately extend the Object class (EK 1.12.A.3). This means every object in Java, regardless of its type, is also an Object.

Declaring Reference Variables (LO 1.12.B)

A reference variable stores the memory address of an object, not the object itself (EK 1.12.B.1). When you declare a reference variable, you specify the class as the type:

String name;        // declares reference variable (currently null)
String greeting = "Hello";  // declares and initializes
Scanner input;      // declares reference variable for Scanner

A reference variable that has not been assigned an object holds the special value null, meaning it doesn't point to any object.

Class vs. Object — An Analogy

// Class = blueprint
// Think: class Cookie defines shape, size, flavor

// Objects = actual cookies made from the blueprint
// cookie1 might be chocolate, cookie2 might be vanilla
// Both are Cookie objects, but with different attribute values
Worked Example 1: Class vs. Object.
// String is a CLASS (the blueprint)
// Each specific String is an OBJECT (an instance)
String s1 = "Hello";   // s1 references a String object
String s2 = "World";   // s2 references a different String object
// Both s1 and s2 are instances of the String class
Worked Example 2: Reference variables hold addresses.
String a = "Hi";
String b = a;  // b now references the SAME object as a
// Both a and b point to the same String object in memory
AP Trap: A reference variable does NOT store the object itself — it stores a memory address (reference) that points to the object. Two variables can reference the same object.
Out of Scope: Designing class hierarchies and inheritance are covered in later units. For now, just know that all classes extend Object.
Summary
  • A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of a class.
  • A class defines attributes and behaviors; an object has specific values for those attributes.
  • All classes in Java extend the Object class (EK 1.12.A.3).
  • A reference variable stores a memory address, not the object itself.
  • An uninitialized reference variable holds null.
  • Multiple reference variables can point to the same object.

problems.question_html: What is the relationship between a class and an object?

choices.text: An object is a blueprint for creating classes
A class is a specific instance of an object
A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance created from it
Classes and objects are the same thing

hints.text: Think of a cookie cutter (class) and the actual cookies (objects).
The class defines the template; objects are created from it with specific values.

solution_steps.text: A class defines the attributes and behaviors that objects will have.
An object is a specific instance of a class with its own attribute values.

problems.question_html: What does a reference variable store?

choices.text: A memory address pointing to the object

hints.text: Reference variables don't hold the object itself.
They hold an address (reference) that points to where the object is stored in memory.

solution_steps.text: Unlike primitive variables that store values directly, reference variables store memory addresses.
The address points to the location in memory where the object is stored.

problems.question_html: Which class is at the root of Java's class hierarchy?

hints.text: All classes in Java ultimately extend this class.
It's the most general class — every Java object is an instance of this class.

solution_steps.text: Java has a class hierarchy where every class inherits from a common ancestor.
The Object class is the root — all classes extend Object either directly or indirectly.

problems.question_html:
After the following code, what is true about a and b?

String a = "Hello";
String b = a;

choices.text: a and b are independent copies of "Hello"
a and b reference the same String object
This code causes a compile error

hints.text: Assigning one reference variable to another copies the address, not the object.
After b = a, both variables point to the same object in memory.

solution_steps.text: String a = "Hello" creates a String object and stores its address in a.
String b = a copies the address from a to b. Both now reference the same object.

problems.question_html: What value does an uninitialized reference variable hold?

hints.text: It's a special value meaning 'no object'.
This 4-letter keyword means the variable doesn't point to any object.

solution_steps.text: When a reference variable is declared but not assigned an object, it holds null.
null means the variable does not reference any object.

problems.question_html: Explain the difference between a class and an object using the Scanner class as an example. Write a declaration that creates a Scanner object and a separate declaration of a Scanner reference variable that holds null.
problems.correct_answer:
// Scanner is the class (blueprint)
// sc is an object (instance) of Scanner
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

// s is a reference variable holding null (no object yet)
Scanner s = null;
rubric: Explains that Scanner is a class (blueprint)
Explains that an object is an instance created from the class
Shows creating a Scanner object with new
Shows a null reference variable declaration

hints.text: A class is a blueprint; an object is a specific instance created from it.
Use 'new Scanner(System.in)' to create an object, or just declare 'Scanner s;' for a null reference.

solution_steps.text: Scanner is a class — it defines what Scanner objects can do (nextInt, nextDouble, etc.).
new Scanner(System.in) creates an object (instance) of that class.
Scanner s = null; declares a reference variable that doesn't point to any object yet.

concepts.title: Object Creation and Storage (Instantiation)
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.13)
  • LO 1.13.A: Identify the constructor signature from documentation.
  • LO 1.13.B: Describe the types of data stored in reference and primitive variables.
  • LO 1.13.C: Create objects using constructors.
TermDefinition
ConstructorA special method called when an object is created; initializes the object's attributes.
newThe keyword used to create (instantiate) a new object.
Overloaded constructorsMultiple constructors with different parameter lists in the same class.
nullA special value indicating a reference variable does not point to any object.
Call by valueJava passes copies of argument values to methods, not the actual variables.

Constructors (LO 1.13.A)

A constructor is a special method that creates and initializes an object (EK 1.13.A.1). Constructors have the same name as the class and have no return type (EK 1.13.A.2). A class can have multiple overloaded constructors with different parameter lists (EK 1.13.A.3).

// Constructor signatures for a Point class:
public Point()                  // no-arg constructor
public Point(int x, int y)      // two-parameter constructor

Reference vs. Primitive Storage (LO 1.13.B)

A reference variable stores a reference (memory address) to an object, or the value null if it doesn't point to any object (EK 1.13.B.1). A primitive variable stores the actual value directly.

Creating Objects (LO 1.13.C)

Objects are created using the new keyword followed by a constructor call (EK 1.13.C.1):

// Syntax: ClassName objectName = new ClassName(arguments);
Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
String greeting = new String("Hello");

When a constructor has parameters, you must pass matching arguments (EK 1.13.C.2, EK 1.13.C.3). Java uses call by value — it passes copies of the argument values, not the original variables (EK 1.13.C.4).

Worked Example 1: Creating objects with constructors.
// Assuming a Rectangle class with two constructors:
// Rectangle() — creates a 0x0 rectangle
// Rectangle(int width, int height) — creates with given dimensions

Rectangle r1 = new Rectangle();        // uses no-arg constructor
Rectangle r2 = new Rectangle(5, 10);   // uses 2-param constructor
Worked Example 2: Reference vs. null.
Scanner s1 = new Scanner(System.in);  // s1 references a Scanner object
Scanner s2 = null;  // s2 is null — no object

// s1 can call methods: s1.nextInt();
// s2.nextInt() would throw NullPointerException!
Worked Example 3: Call by value.
int x = 5;
// When passing x to a method, Java copies the value 5
// The method gets its own copy; changing it won't affect x
someMethod(x);  // x is still 5 after the call
AP Trap: Calling a method on a null reference throws a NullPointerException. Always make sure your reference variable points to an actual object.
AP Trap: Java is call by value. Primitive arguments are copied. For reference types, the reference (address) is copied, not the object.
Summary
  • A constructor initializes a new object; it has the same name as the class and no return type.
  • Use new ClassName(args) to create objects.
  • Classes can have overloaded constructors with different parameter lists.
  • Reference variables store an address or null.
  • Java uses call by value — arguments are copies, not originals.
  • Calling a method on null causes NullPointerException.

problems.question_html: Which keyword is used to create a new object in Java?

hints.text: This keyword is used with a constructor call.
The syntax is: new ClassName(arguments).

solution_steps.text: Objects are created using the 'new' keyword followed by a constructor.
Example: Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

problems.question_html: What is true about constructors?

choices.text: They must have a return type
They have the same name as the class and no return type
A class can have only one constructor

hints.text: Constructors are special — they match the class name.
Constructors have no return type (not even void) and must match the class name.

solution_steps.text: Constructors are named after their class and do not have a return type.
A class can have multiple overloaded constructors with different parameter lists.

problems.question_html: Given a class Car with constructors Car() and Car(String make, int year), which creates a Car with make "Toyota" and year 2024?

hints.text: Use the new keyword with matching argument types.
The constructor takes a String first and an int second.

solution_steps.text: Use new with the constructor that takes (String, int).
new Car("Toyota", 2024) matches Car(String make, int year).

problems.question_html: What does "call by value" mean in Java?

choices.text: Methods can change the original variables passed to them
Java passes the memory address of all arguments
Java passes copies of argument values; the original variables are not changed
Java does not allow passing arguments to methods

hints.text: Think about whether the method gets the original or a copy.
Java copies the value (for primitives) or reference (for objects) — the original variable is unchanged.

solution_steps.text: Call by value means Java copies the argument value into the parameter.
For primitives, the copy is the actual value. For references, the copy is the address.
In both cases, the original variable in the calling code is not modified.

problems.question_html: What exception is thrown when you try to call a method on a null reference?

hints.text: This exception is thrown when a reference variable doesn't point to an object.
It starts with 'Null' and ends with 'Exception'.

solution_steps.text: When a reference variable is null, it doesn't point to any object.
Calling a method on null throws a NullPointerException.

problems.question_html:
A class Student has two constructors:

  • Student(String name) — creates a student with the given name and GPA 0.0
  • Student(String name, double gpa) — creates a student with the given name and GPA

Write Java code that creates two Student objects: one named "Alice" with default GPA, and one named "Bob" with GPA 3.8. Store them in variables s1 and s2.
problems.correct_answer:
Student s1 = new Student("Alice");
Student s2 = new Student("Bob", 3.8);
rubric: Creates s1 using the one-parameter constructor
Creates s2 using the two-parameter constructor
Uses new keyword for both
Arguments match the constructor parameter types

hints.text: Match the arguments to the constructor parameters.
s1 uses Student(String) and s2 uses Student(String, double).

solution_steps.text: s1 = new Student("Alice") uses the one-parameter constructor.
s2 = new Student("Bob", 3.8) uses the two-parameter constructor with name and GPA.

concepts.title: Calling Instance Methods
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.14)
  • LO 1.14.A: Call instance methods and determine the result.
TermDefinition
Instance methodA non-static method that is called on a specific object.
Dot operator (.)Used to call an instance method on an object: object.method().
NullPointerExceptionThrown when calling a method on a null reference.
Accessor methodA method that returns information about an object without modifying it (getter).
Mutator methodA method that modifies the object's attributes (setter).

Instance Methods vs. Class Methods (LO 1.14.A)

Instance methods are called on specific objects using the dot operator (EK 1.14.A.1). Unlike static (class) methods, instance methods require an object to act upon:

// Instance methods — called on objects
String s = "Hello World";
int len = s.length();          // 11 — called on object s
String upper = s.toUpperCase(); // "HELLO WORLD"

// Static methods — called on the class
int abs = Math.abs(-5);        // called on the Math class

The key distinction: s.length() needs the specific string object s to know which string's length to return.

NullPointerException (EK 1.14.A.2)

If you try to call an instance method on a reference that is null, Java throws a NullPointerException:

String s = null;
int len = s.length();  // NullPointerException!

This is one of the most common run-time errors in Java.

Accessor vs. Mutator Methods

Accessor methods (getters) return information without changing the object. Mutator methods (setters) change the object's state:

// Accessor: length() returns info, doesn't change the string
String s = "Hello";
int len = s.length();  // 5 — s is unchanged

// Mutator example (ArrayList):
ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("item");  // mutator — changes the list
Worked Example 1: Chaining instance methods.
String name = "  Alice  ";
String cleaned = name.trim().toUpperCase();
System.out.println(cleaned);  // "ALICE"

name.trim() returns "Alice", then .toUpperCase() is called on that result.

Worked Example 2: Accessor methods on String.
String word = "Java";
System.out.println(word.length());      // 4
System.out.println(word.indexOf("va")); // 2
System.out.println(word.substring(1));   // "ava"
AP Trap: NullPointerException is one of the most commonly tested exceptions. Always check: is the reference variable null before calling methods on it?
AP Trap: Instance methods are called on objects (s.length()), while class methods are called on classes (Math.abs()). Don't confuse the two.
Summary
  • Instance methods are called on objects: object.method().
  • They require a specific object to operate on (unlike static methods).
  • Calling an instance method on null throws NullPointerException.
  • Accessor methods return info without changing the object.
  • Mutator methods change the object's state.
  • Methods can be chained: obj.method1().method2().

concepts.title: String Manipulation
concepts.content_html:
What You'll Learn (CED 1.15)
  • LO 1.15.A: Create String objects and use concatenation.
  • LO 1.15.B: Call String methods and determine the result.
TermDefinition
StringA reference type representing a sequence of characters. Part of java.lang.
ImmutableOnce a String is created, its contents cannot be changed.
ConcatenationJoining strings together using the + or += operator.
IndexThe position of a character in a string, starting from 0.
length()Returns the number of characters in the string.
substring()Returns a portion of the string.
indexOf()Returns the index of the first occurrence of a substring, or -1 if not found.
equals()Compares two strings for content equality (case-sensitive).

Creating Strings (LO 1.15.A)

String is a reference type in java.lang — no import needed (EK 1.15.A.1, EK 1.15.A.2). Strings are immutable — once created, their characters cannot be changed (EK 1.15.A.3). Any method that seems to modify a String actually creates a new String.

String s1 = "Hello";                // string literal
String s2 = new String("Hello");     // using constructor (less common)

String Concatenation (EK 1.15.A.4)

The + operator joins strings together. When one operand is a String, the other is automatically converted to a String:

String greeting = "Hello" + " " + "World";  // "Hello World"
int age = 17;
String msg = "Age: " + age;  // "Age: 17" (int converted to String)

// += also works for concatenation:
String result = "A";
result += "B";  // result is now "AB"

The toString() Method (EK 1.15.A.5)

When an object is concatenated with a String using +, Java automatically calls the object's toString() method to convert it to a String representation.

String Methods (LO 1.15.B)

String characters are indexed from 0 to length()-1 (EK 1.15.B.1). Key methods (EK 1.15.B.2):

String s = "Hello World";

// length() — number of characters
s.length()               // 11

// substring(int from, int to) — characters from index 'from' up to but NOT including 'to'
s.substring(0, 5)        // "Hello"
s.substring(6)           // "World" (from index 6 to end)

// indexOf(String str) — first occurrence, or -1 if not found
s.indexOf("World")       // 6
s.indexOf("xyz")         // -1

// equals(String other) — compares content (case-sensitive)
s.equals("Hello World")  // true
s.equals("hello world")  // false

// compareTo(String other) — lexicographic comparison
"apple".compareTo("banana")  // negative (apple < banana)
"banana".compareTo("apple")  // positive (banana > apple)
"cat".compareTo("cat")       // 0 (equal)

Extracting Single Characters (EK 1.15.B.3)

To extract a single character as a String, use substring(i, i+1):

String s = "Java";
String first = s.substring(0, 1);   // "J"
String last = s.substring(s.length() - 1);  // "a"
Worked Example 1: String concatenation with numbers.
int x = 3, y = 4;
System.out.println("Sum: " + x + y);     // "Sum: 34" (concatenation, not addition!)
System.out.println("Sum: " + (x + y));   // "Sum: 7" (parentheses force addition first)

Without parentheses, "Sum: " + x produces "Sum: 3", then "Sum: 3" + y produces "Sum: 34".

Worked Example 2: Using substring and indexOf.
String email = "student@school.edu";
int atSign = email.indexOf("@");       // 7
String user = email.substring(0, atSign);  // "student"
String domain = email.substring(atSign + 1); // "school.edu"
System.out.println(user);    // student
System.out.println(domain);  // school.edu
AP Trap: "Sum: " + 3 + 4 produces "Sum: 34" (string concatenation), NOT "Sum: 7". Use parentheses to force arithmetic: "Sum: " + (3 + 4).
AP Trap: Use .equals() to compare String content, NOT ==. The == operator compares references (memory addresses), not the actual characters.
AP Trap: substring(a, b) includes index a but excludes index b. It returns characters from index a up to (but not including) b.
Summary
  • Strings are immutable reference types in java.lang (no import needed).
  • + concatenates strings; non-String values are auto-converted.
  • String indices go from 0 to length()-1.
  • substring(a, b) — from a (inclusive) to b (exclusive).
  • indexOf(str) — returns first position or -1 if not found.
  • equals() — compares content; compareTo() — lexicographic ordering.
  • Use substring(i, i+1) to get a single character as a String.
  • Always use .equals(), not ==, to compare String content.
