Inner loop: for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) { print(j + " "); }
After inner loop, println() moves to next line.

concepts.title: Informal Run-Time Analysis
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 2.12)
  • LO 2.12.A: Determine how many times a statement executes in a program.
TermDefinition
Statement execution countThe number of times a particular statement is executed during a program run.
TracingManually following the flow of a program to track variable values and execution counts.
Constant timeA section of code that always executes a fixed number of times, regardless of input size.
Linear timeExecution count grows proportionally with the input size (single loop over n items).
Quadratic timeExecution count grows proportionally with the square of input size (nested loops).

Counting Statement Executions (EK 2.12.A.1)

The execution count of a statement indicates how many times that statement is executed during a program run. You can determine this through tracing (manually following the code) and analysis (reasoning about loop bounds) (EK 2.12.A.1).

Sequential Statements

A statement outside any loop executes exactly once.

int x = 5;              // executes 1 time
System.out.println(x);  // executes 1 time

Single Loop

A statement inside a loop that runs n times executes n times.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);  // executes n times
}

Nested Loops

A statement inside nested loops: multiply the iteration counts of all enclosing loops.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        System.out.println("*");  // executes n * n = n² times
    }
}

Conditional Inside a Loop

A statement inside an if within a loop might not execute every iteration:

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        System.out.println(i);  // executes 5 times (0,2,4,6,8)
    }
}
Worked Example 1: Count executions.
int count = 0;                    // 1 time
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {   // loop runs 4 times
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) { // inner runs 3 times per outer
        count++;                   // 4 * 3 = 12 times
    }
}
System.out.println(count);       // 1 time

count++ executes 12 times. The println executes once. Output: 12

Worked Example 2: Dependent inner loop.
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
        total++;  // how many times?
    }
}

i=1: 1 time. i=2: 2 times. i=3: 3. i=4: 4. i=5: 5. Total: 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 executions.

AP Trap: When asked "how many times does this statement execute?", students often count loop iterations incorrectly. Be precise about the loop bounds: does the loop use < or <=? Start from 0 or 1?
Summary
  • Sequential: each statement runs once.
  • Single loop of n: statements inside run n times.
  • Nested loops: multiply iteration counts of all enclosing loops.
  • Conditional inside loop: count only the iterations where the condition is true.
  • Dependent inner loop: sum the inner counts for each outer iteration.
  • Determine counts through tracing (manual) or analysis (reasoning).

problems.question_html:
How many times does the statement x++ execute?

int x = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 4; j++) {
        x++;
    }
}

hints.text: Outer loop: 5 times. Inner loop: 4 times each.

solution_steps.text: Outer loop runs 5 times (i=0 to 4). Inner loop runs 4 times each (j=0 to 3).
x++ executes 5 * 4 = 20 times.

problems.question_html:
How many times does the print statement execute?

for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    if (i % 3 == 0) {
        System.out.println(i);
    }
}

hints.text: Which values of i from 0 to 5 are divisible by 3?
0 % 3 == 0 and 3 % 3 == 0. That's 2 times.

solution_steps.text: The print executes 2 times.

problems.question_html:
How many times does the inner print execute?

for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + "," + j);
    }
}

hints.text: Two independent loops each running n times.
Nested: n outer * n inner = n^2.

solution_steps.text: Outer loop: n iterations. Inner loop: n iterations for each outer.
Total: n * n = n^2 executions.

problems.question_html: A single for loop runs from i = 0 to i < n. How many times does a statement inside the loop body execute (in terms of n)?

hints.text: i takes values 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1.
That's n values total.

solution_steps.text: The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1. That is n iterations.
A statement inside executes n times.

problems.question_html:
How many times does the statement count++ execute?

int count = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {
        count++;
    }
}

hints.text: The inner loop depends on i. Sum the inner counts.
i=1: 1 time. i=2: 2 times. i=3: 3 times. Total: 6.

solution_steps.text: i=1: j runs 1 time. i=2: 2 times. i=3: 3 times.

problems.question_html:
What is the value of count after this code runs?

int count = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    for (int j = i; j <= 4; j++) {
        count++;
    }
}

hints.text: j starts at i and goes to 4. Count iterations for each i.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following code segment. Determine how many times each labeled statement executes and explain your reasoning.

int x = 0;                        // Statement A
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {    // Statement B (the loop header)
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++) {
        if (j < 2) {
            x++;                  // Statement C
        }
    }
}
problems.correct_answer:
Statement A: Executes 1 time (sequential, outside loops).

Statement B: The outer loop runs 3 times (i=0,1,2).

Statement C: For each outer iteration, the inner loop runs 5 times (j=0-4). The condition j < 2 is true for j=0 and j=1, so x++ runs 2 times per outer iteration. Total: 3 * 2 = 6 times.
rubric: Correctly identifies Statement A executes 1 time
Correctly identifies the outer loop runs 3 times
Correctly identifies Statement C runs 2 times per outer iteration (j < 2)
Correctly calculates total: 3 * 2 = 6 for Statement C

hints.text: Analyze each statement separately. Consider which loops enclose it.
For Statement C, you need both the loop count AND the condition. j < 2 is true for j=0,1 only.

solution_steps.text: Statement A: outside all loops, runs 1 time.
Statement B (outer loop): runs 3 times (i=0,1,2).
Statement C: inside both loops. Inner runs 5 times per outer, but j < 2 is true only for j=0,1 (2 times). So C runs 3 * 2 = 6 times.

topics.name: Unit 3: Class Creation
topics.description: Object-oriented programming: designing classes with instance variables, constructors, methods (accessor and mutator), static members, scope, encapsulation, and the this keyword.

concepts.title: Abstraction and Program Design
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.1)
  • LO 3.1.A: Represent program design using natural language or diagrams.
TermDefinition
AbstractionReducing complexity by hiding irrelevant details and exposing only essential features.
Data abstractionSeparating abstract properties of a data type from its concrete representation.
AttributeA data abstraction defined within a class; represented as an instance or class variable.
Instance variableA variable whose value is unique to each object instance.
Class variableA variable shared among all instances of a class (declared with static).
Procedural abstractionGiving a name to a process so it can be invoked without knowing internal details.
Method decompositionBreaking a complex behavior into smaller, reusable methods.

What Is Abstraction? (LO 3.1.A)

Abstraction is one of the most powerful tools in computer science. It reduces complexity by hiding irrelevant details and letting you focus on the big picture (EK 3.1.A.1). When you drive a car, you use the steering wheel and pedals without understanding how the engine works internally. Programming works the same way.

Data Abstraction (EK 3.1.A.2 – EK 3.1.A.3)

Data abstraction separates what data represents from how it is stored (EK 3.1.A.2). In Java, a class defines abstract properties using attributes. An attribute is a data abstraction within a class (EK 3.1.A.3).

There are two kinds of attributes:

  • Instance variables — each object gets its own copy (EK 3.1.A.3).
  • Class variables — shared across all instances, declared with static (EK 3.1.A.3).
public class Dog {
    private String name;       // instance variable
    private int age;           // instance variable
    private static int count;  // class variable
}

Procedural Abstraction (EK 3.1.A.4 – EK 3.1.A.6)

Procedural abstraction means giving a name to a sequence of steps so others can call it without knowing the internal details (EK 3.1.A.4). Method decomposition is the practice of breaking a large behavior into smaller methods, each handling one task (EK 3.1.A.4). When multiple methods share similar steps, you can extract those shared features into a single reusable method (EK 3.1.A.4).

Parameters make procedures more general and reusable (EK 3.1.A.5). Instead of writing separate methods for every variation, you pass data in as parameters.

A key benefit: you can change a method’s internal implementation without affecting code that calls it, as long as the method signature stays the same (EK 3.1.A.6).

Designing Before Coding (EK 3.1.A.7)

Before writing code, design your classes by identifying their attributes (data) and behaviors (methods) (EK 3.1.A.7). Use natural language descriptions, diagrams, or pseudocode to plan. For example, a BankAccount class might have attributes balance and owner, and behaviors deposit, withdraw, and getBalance.

Worked Example 1: Design a Student class.

Attributes: name (String), gradeLevel (int), gpa (double).

Behaviors: getName(), getGpa(), setGpa(double newGpa), isHonorRoll().

This is data abstraction — we defined what a Student has and does without writing any implementation code yet.

Worked Example 2: Method decomposition.
public class ReportCard {
    public void printReport(Student s) {
        printHeader(s);
        printGrades(s);
        printSummary(s);
    }
    private void printHeader(Student s) { /* ... */ }
    private void printGrades(Student s) { /* ... */ }
    private void printSummary(Student s) { /* ... */ }
}

The printReport method is decomposed into three smaller methods, each handling one part of the task (EK 3.1.A.4).

AP Trap: Abstraction is not just about hiding code — it is about reducing complexity. On the AP exam, focus on why abstraction matters, not just how it is implemented.
Summary
  • Abstraction reduces complexity by hiding irrelevant details (EK 3.1.A.1).
  • Data abstraction separates what data represents from how it is stored (EK 3.1.A.2).
  • Instance variables are unique per object; class variables are shared (EK 3.1.A.3).
  • Procedural abstraction names a process; method decomposition breaks it into smaller pieces (EK 3.1.A.4).
  • Parameters generalize procedures for reuse (EK 3.1.A.5).
  • Changing internals without changing the signature preserves abstraction (EK 3.1.A.6).
  • Design classes with attributes and behaviors before writing code (EK 3.1.A.7).

problems.question_html: Which of the following best describes data abstraction?

choices.text: Writing code that runs as fast as possible
Separating abstract properties of data from its concrete representation
Using loops to repeat a block of code

hints.text: Think about what 'abstraction' means — hiding details.
Data abstraction is about separating what data represents from how it is stored.

solution_steps.text: Data abstraction separates the abstract properties (what the data represents) from the concrete representation (how it is stored in memory).
This is EK 3.1.A.2. The other options describe unrelated concepts.

problems.question_html: A programmer changes the internal algorithm of a method but keeps its name, parameters, and return type the same. Which principle does this illustrate?

hints.text: The method signature (name + parameters) did not change.
Procedural abstraction lets you change internals without affecting callers (EK 3.1.A.6).

solution_steps.text: Procedural abstraction means users of a method do not need to know how it works internally.
As long as the method signature is preserved, internal changes are invisible to callers (EK 3.1.A.6).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a benefit of using parameters in methods?

choices.text: Parameters allow methods to be more general and reusable
Parameters prevent all errors in a method

hints.text: Think about what happens if you hardcode all values instead of using parameters.
Parameters generalize procedures for reuse (EK 3.1.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Without parameters, you would need a separate method for every specific case.
Parameters let you write one method that works for many inputs, making it general and reusable (EK 3.1.A.5).

problems.question_html: A class variable declared with static is shared by how many objects of that class?

choices.text: Only objects in the same method
No objects; only the class itself can use it

hints.text: Think about the word 'class variable' — it belongs to the class, not individual objects.
A class variable is shared among ALL instances of the class (EK 3.1.A.3).

solution_steps.text: A class variable (static) has one copy shared among all instances of the class (EK 3.1.A.3).
Changing it from one object affects all objects because they share the same variable.

problems.question_html: A variable whose value is unique to each object instance is called a(n) _____ variable.

hints.text: Each object gets its own copy of this type of variable.
It is the opposite of a class (static) variable.

solution_steps.text: An instance variable belongs to a specific object and each object has its own copy (EK 3.1.A.3).
A class variable, declared with static, is shared among all instances.

problems.question_html: Breaking a complex method into several smaller, more focused methods is called method _____.

hints.text: Think about the word that means 'breaking down into parts.'
Method _____ breaks large behaviors into smaller, reusable methods (EK 3.1.A.4).

solution_steps.text: Method decomposition is the practice of breaking a complex behavior into smaller methods, each handling one responsibility (EK 3.1.A.4).
This makes code easier to read, test, and reuse.

concepts.title: Impact of Program Design
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.2)
  • LO 3.2.A: Explain the social and ethical implications of computing systems.
TermDefinition
System reliabilityThe ability of a program to perform its intended tasks consistently and correctly.
Intellectual propertyCreations of the mind (code, algorithms, designs) that may be legally protected.
Open sourceSoftware whose source code is freely available for anyone to view, modify, and distribute.
Non-open sourceProprietary software whose source code is not shared publicly.
TestingThe process of running a program with various inputs to verify correct behavior.

System Reliability (EK 3.2.A.1)

System reliability means a program performs its intended tasks as expected under a variety of conditions (EK 3.2.A.1). Reliable software does not crash unexpectedly, does not produce incorrect results, and handles edge cases gracefully. Testing is the primary way to maximize system reliability (EK 3.2.A.1). This includes testing with normal inputs, boundary values, and invalid inputs.

Impact on Society (EK 3.2.A.2)

Programs have wide-reaching effects on society, the economy, and culture — both beneficial and harmful (EK 3.2.A.2). Beneficial examples include medical software that saves lives, navigation apps that reduce travel time, and educational tools that make learning accessible. Harmful examples include privacy violations through data collection, algorithmic bias in hiring or lending, and addictive social media features.

As a programmer, you have an ethical responsibility to consider how your software affects real people.

Legal and Intellectual Property Issues (EK 3.2.A.3)

Software development raises important legal issues around intellectual property (EK 3.2.A.3). Code you write may be protected by copyright. Using someone else’s code without permission can be illegal.

Open source software makes its source code freely available. Anyone can view, modify, and distribute it (EK 3.2.A.3). Examples include Linux and the Java Development Kit. Non-open source (proprietary) software keeps its source code secret (EK 3.2.A.3). You may use it but cannot see or modify the source code.

Always read and follow software licenses. Even open source software has license terms that must be respected.

Worked Example 1: Reliability through testing.

A banking app processes transfers. To ensure reliability, testers should verify:

  • Normal transfer: $100 from account A to account B
  • Boundary: transfer of $0.00
  • Edge case: transfer amount exceeds balance
  • Concurrent: two transfers at the same time

Each test increases confidence that the system is reliable (EK 3.2.A.1).

Worked Example 2: Ethical considerations.

A school uses an algorithm to assign students to classes. If the algorithm unintentionally groups students by socioeconomic status, it could create inequity. The programmer should test the algorithm for fairness and bias (EK 3.2.A.2).

AP Trap: The AP exam may ask you to identify whether a scenario describes a beneficial or harmful impact. Remember that the same technology can be both — a face recognition system helps find missing persons but can also enable surveillance.
Summary
  • System reliability means performing tasks as expected; maximize through testing (EK 3.2.A.1).
  • Programs impact society, economy, and culture — both positively and negatively (EK 3.2.A.2).
  • Intellectual property and legal issues apply to software development (EK 3.2.A.3).
  • Open source code is freely available; non-open source code is proprietary (EK 3.2.A.3).
  • Programmers have an ethical duty to consider the impact of their code on people.

problems.question_html: Which of the following best describes system reliability?

choices.text: The speed at which a program executes
The ability of a program to perform its intended tasks as expected
The number of lines of code in a program
The amount of memory a program uses

hints.text: Reliability is about consistency and correctness, not speed.
A reliable system performs its intended tasks correctly and consistently (EK 3.2.A.1).

solution_steps.text: System reliability refers to a program's ability to perform its intended tasks as expected (EK 3.2.A.1).
It is maximized through thorough testing with various inputs.

problems.question_html: A social media algorithm recommends content that keeps users engaged for long periods. This is an example of a program having what kind of impact?

choices.text: Only a beneficial impact on society
Only a harmful impact on society
Both a beneficial and harmful impact on society

hints.text: Engagement can be good (connecting people) and bad (addiction).
Programs can have both beneficial and harmful impacts on society (EK 3.2.A.2).

solution_steps.text: The algorithm benefits users by showing relevant content and connecting people.
It can also harm users through addiction and reduced well-being. Programs often have both positive and negative impacts (EK 3.2.A.2).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is true about intellectual property in software development?

choices.text: All code found online can be freely used without restrictions
Open source software has no license terms
Using someone else's code without permission can have legal consequences
Only compiled code is protected by copyright

hints.text: Think about what 'intellectual property' means — creative works that are legally protected.
Code is a creative work and may be protected by copyright (EK 3.2.A.3).

solution_steps.text: Intellectual property laws protect code. Using code without permission can be illegal (EK 3.2.A.3).
Even open source software has license terms. Source code, not just compiled code, is protected.

problems.question_html: A programmer discovers that their sorting algorithm produces incorrect results when the input list is empty. This is a failure of which quality?

hints.text: The program does not perform its intended task correctly for an edge case.
System reliability means performing tasks as expected — including edge cases (EK 3.2.A.1).

solution_steps.text: The program fails to handle an edge case (empty list), which means it does not reliably perform its task.
This is a reliability issue. Testing with edge cases would have caught this (EK 3.2.A.1).

problems.question_html: Software whose source code is freely available for anyone to view, modify, and distribute is called _____ source software.

hints.text: The source code is available for anyone to see — it is not hidden or closed.
_____ source means the code is publicly accessible (EK 3.2.A.3).

solution_steps.text: Open source software makes its source code freely available for viewing, modifying, and distributing (EK 3.2.A.3).
Non-open source (proprietary) software keeps its source code secret.

problems.question_html: The primary way to maximize system reliability is through _____.

hints.text: You need to verify the program works correctly with various inputs.
Running the program with normal, boundary, and invalid inputs is called _____ (EK 3.2.A.1).

solution_steps.text: Testing is the primary way to maximize system reliability (EK 3.2.A.1).
Good testing includes normal inputs, boundary values, and edge cases.

concepts.title: Anatomy of a Class
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.3)
  • LO 3.3.A: Designate access and visibility constraints to the declaration of a class, constructors, methods, and instance variables.
TermDefinition
EncapsulationHiding implementation details and restricting direct access to an object's data.
publicAccess modifier allowing access from any class.
privateAccess modifier restricting access to within the declaring class only.
classKeyword used to declare a class in Java.
Access modifierA keyword (public or private) that controls visibility.

Encapsulation (EK 3.3.A.1)

Encapsulation is the practice of hiding the internal details of a class from outside code (EK 3.3.A.1). Java enforces encapsulation through access modifiers: public and private. These keywords control which parts of a class are visible to other classes.

Think of encapsulation like a capsule — the medicine (implementation) is hidden inside, and you interact with it only through the approved interface (public methods).

Class Declarations (EK 3.3.A.2)

A class is declared using the class keyword and is designated public (EK 3.3.A.2). A public class can be accessed from any other class.

public class Rectangle {
    // instance variables, constructors, and methods go here
}

Constructors (EK 3.3.A.3)

Constructors are designated public so that other classes can create objects of the class (EK 3.3.A.3). A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type.

Instance Variables (EK 3.3.A.4 – EK 3.3.A.5)

Instance variables belong to the object — each object gets its own copy of every instance variable (EK 3.3.A.4). Instance variables should be declared private to enforce encapsulation (EK 3.3.A.5). This prevents outside code from directly accessing or modifying the data.

Methods: public vs. private (EK 3.3.A.6)

public methods can be called from any class — they form the external interface of the class (EK 3.3.A.6). private methods can only be called from within the same class — they are helper methods used internally (EK 3.3.A.6).

public class Rectangle {
    private double length;  // private instance variable
    private double width;   // private instance variable

    public Rectangle(double l, double w) {  // public constructor
        length = l;
        width = w;
    }

    public double getArea() {  // public method
        return length * width;
    }

    private double diagonal() {  // private helper method
        return Math.sqrt(length * length + width * width);
    }
}
Worked Example 1: Identifying access levels.
public class Circle {
    private double radius;

    public Circle(double r) {
        radius = r;
    }

    public double getRadius() {
        return radius;
    }
}

Circle is public (accessible everywhere). radius is private (only accessible inside Circle). The constructor and getRadius() are public (callable from other classes).

Worked Example 2: Why private matters.
Circle c = new Circle(5.0);
// c.radius = -10;  // COMPILE ERROR: radius is private
double r = c.getRadius();  // OK: getRadius() is public

Making radius private prevents invalid values. The class controls access through its public methods.

AP Trap: Instance variables should always be private on the AP exam. If you see a question where instance variables are public, that violates encapsulation.
AP Trap: A private method cannot be called from outside the class. If the AP exam shows code calling a private method from another class, it will not compile.
Summary
  • Encapsulation hides implementation details using access modifiers (EK 3.3.A.1).
  • Classes are declared public with the class keyword (EK 3.3.A.2).
  • Constructors are public (EK 3.3.A.3).
  • Each object has its own copy of instance variables (EK 3.3.A.4).
  • Instance variables should be private (EK 3.3.A.5).
  • public methods are accessible externally; private methods are internal only (EK 3.3.A.6).

problems.question_html: Which access modifier should be used for instance variables to enforce encapsulation?

hints.text: Encapsulation means hiding data from outside access.
Instance variables should be declared private (EK 3.3.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Encapsulation requires hiding instance variables from outside code.
The private modifier restricts access to within the class only (EK 3.3.A.5).

problems.question_html:
Consider the following code:

public class Dog {
    private String name;
    public Dog(String n) { name = n; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
}

// In another class:
Dog d = new Dog("Rex");
System.out.println(d.name);

What happens when this code is compiled?

choices.text: Compile error: name has private access in Dog

hints.text: Look at the access modifier on the name variable.
name is private — it cannot be accessed directly from another class (EK 3.3.A.5).

solution_steps.text: The variable name is declared private, so it cannot be accessed from outside the Dog class.
Accessing d.name from another class causes a compile error. You must use d.getName() instead (EK 3.3.A.6).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is true about private methods?

choices.text: They can be called from any class
They can only be called from within the same class

hints.text: Private means restricted to the declaring class.
Private methods are only callable from within the same class (EK 3.3.A.6).

solution_steps.text: A private method can only be called from within the class that declares it (EK 3.3.A.6).
Private methods serve as helper methods for the class's public interface.

problems.question_html: The practice of hiding a class's internal details and restricting direct access to its data is called _____.

hints.text: Think of a capsule that hides what is inside.
This OOP principle uses public/private access modifiers (EK 3.3.A.1).

solution_steps.text: Encapsulation hides implementation details by using access modifiers to restrict direct access (EK 3.3.A.1).
Private instance variables and public methods are the standard pattern.

problems.question_html: In Java, classes are declared using the _____ keyword.

hints.text: It is a reserved word that defines a new type.
public _____ ClassName { } (EK 3.3.A.2).

solution_steps.text: The class keyword is used to declare a class in Java (EK 3.3.A.2).
Classes are typically designated public so they can be accessed from other classes.

problems.question_html: Write a complete class header and one private instance variable declaration for a class called Book with a private instance variable title of type String.
problems.correct_answer:
public class Book {
    private String title;
}
rubric: Class is declared public with the class keyword
Class name is Book (correct capitalization)
Instance variable title is declared private
Instance variable type is String

hints.text: A class declaration starts with public class ClassName.
Instance variables should be private for encapsulation (EK 3.3.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Declare the class as public class Book (EK 3.3.A.2).
Inside the class body, declare the instance variable as private String title (EK 3.3.A.5).
The private modifier ensures encapsulation — title cannot be accessed directly from other classes.

concepts.title: Constructors
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.4)
  • LO 3.4.A: Declare instance variables and initialize using a constructor with parameters.
TermDefinition
ConstructorA special method that initializes an object's state when it is created.
Object stateThe set of values stored in an object's instance variables at a given time.
has-a relationshipAn object 'has' attributes defined by its instance variables.
Default constructorA no-parameter constructor automatically provided by Java when no constructor is written.
Default valuesInitial values assigned by Java: int=0, double=0.0, boolean=false, reference=null.
Mutable objectAn object whose state can be changed after creation.

Object State and Instance Variables (EK 3.4.A.1)

An object’s state consists of all the attributes and their current values (EK 3.4.A.1). Instance variables define a has-a relationship: a Student object has a name, has a gpa, etc. (EK 3.4.A.1).

Constructors (EK 3.4.A.2)

A constructor sets the initial state of an object (EK 3.4.A.2). When you create an object with new, Java allocates memory and calls the constructor, which returns a reference to the new object (EK 3.4.A.2). Constructor parameters provide the data needed to initialize instance variables.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    private double gpa;

    public Student(String studentName, double studentGpa) {
        name = studentName;
        gpa = studentGpa;
    }
}

Mutable Object Parameters (EK 3.4.A.3)

When a mutable object is passed as a constructor parameter, you should initialize the instance variable with a copy of the object, not the original reference (EK 3.4.A.3). Otherwise, changes to the original object outside the class would change the object’s state unexpectedly.

public class Roster {
    private ArrayList<String> names;

    public Roster(ArrayList<String> nameList) {
        names = new ArrayList<String>(nameList);  // copy!
    }
}

Default Constructor (EK 3.4.A.4 – EK 3.4.A.5)

If you do not write any constructor, Java provides a default no-parameter constructor that initializes all instance variables to their default values (EK 3.4.A.4):

  • int → 0
  • double → 0.0
  • boolean → false
  • Reference types → null

(EK 3.4.A.5)

Important: If you write any constructor, Java does NOT provide the default constructor automatically. You must write it yourself if you want a no-parameter constructor.

Worked Example 1: Writing a constructor.
public class BankAccount {
    private String owner;
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(String ownerName, double initialBalance) {
        owner = ownerName;
        balance = initialBalance;
    }
}

// Usage:
BankAccount acct = new BankAccount("Alice", 1000.0);

The constructor sets owner to "Alice" and balance to 1000.0.

Worked Example 2: Default values.
public class Counter {
    private int count;
    private boolean active;
    private String label;
    // No constructor written
}

Counter c = new Counter();
// c.count == 0, c.active == false, c.label == null

Since no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-parameter constructor. All fields get default values (EK 3.4.A.4, EK 3.4.A.5).

AP Trap: If you write ANY constructor (even one with parameters), Java no longer provides the default no-parameter constructor. Calling new ClassName() without a matching constructor causes a compile error.
AP Trap: Default value for a boolean is false, not true. Default for a reference type is null, not an empty object.
Summary
  • Object state = values of all instance variables; defines has-a relationships (EK 3.4.A.1).
  • Constructors set initial state, allocate memory, return a reference (EK 3.4.A.2).
  • Copy mutable objects passed to constructors to prevent aliasing bugs (EK 3.4.A.3).
  • No constructor written → Java provides a default no-parameter constructor (EK 3.4.A.4).
  • Default values: int=0, double=0.0, boolean=false, reference=null (EK 3.4.A.5).
  • Writing any constructor removes the default constructor.

problems.question_html: What is the default value of an int instance variable that is not explicitly initialized?

hints.text: Java assigns default values to uninitialized instance variables.
The default value for int is 0 (EK 3.4.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Java initializes uninitialized int instance variables to 0 (EK 3.4.A.5).
Other defaults: double=0.0, boolean=false, reference types=null.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following class:

public class Pet {
    private String species;
    private int age;

    public Pet(String s, int a) {
        species = s;
        age = a;
    }
}

Which of the following correctly creates a Pet object?

hints.text: Look at the constructor's parameter list: it requires a String and an int.
Since a constructor is written, there is no default no-parameter constructor (EK 3.4.A.4).

solution_steps.text: The constructor requires two parameters: a String and an int. Only option B provides both.
Option A fails because no no-parameter constructor exists. Option C is missing the new keyword. Option D has only one argument.

problems.question_html: Why should you initialize a mutable object parameter with a copy in the constructor?

choices.text: To prevent outside code from modifying the object's internal state
To make the constructor run faster
Because Java requires it for all parameters

hints.text: If you store the original reference, outside code still points to the same object.
Storing a copy protects the object's state from unintended external changes (EK 3.4.A.3).

solution_steps.text: If the constructor stores the original reference, the caller still has access to the same object.
Changes made by the caller would modify the object's internal state, violating encapsulation (EK 3.4.A.3).
Creating a copy ensures the object controls its own state.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following class:

public class Temp {
    private double value;
    private String scale;
}

What is the value of scale after new Temp() is called?

hints.text: No constructor is written, so Java provides a default one.
The default value for a reference type like String is null (EK 3.4.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Since no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-parameter constructor (EK 3.4.A.4).
String is a reference type, so its default value is null, not an empty string (EK 3.4.A.5).

problems.question_html: When no constructor is explicitly written, Java provides a default _____ constructor.

hints.text: This default constructor takes no arguments.
It is a constructor with zero parameters (EK 3.4.A.4).

solution_steps.text: Java provides a default no-parameter constructor when no constructor is written (EK 3.4.A.4).
This constructor initializes all instance variables to their default values (EK 3.4.A.5).

problems.question_html: The default value of a boolean instance variable is _____.

hints.text: boolean can only be true or false. Which is the default?
The default for boolean is false (EK 3.4.A.5).

solution_steps.text: Java initializes uninitialized boolean instance variables to false (EK 3.4.A.5).
This is a common AP exam question — remember boolean defaults to false, not true.

problems.question_html: Write a complete class called Book with private instance variables title (String) and pages (int), and a constructor that takes parameters to initialize both variables.
problems.correct_answer:
public class Book {
    private String title;
    private int pages;

    public Book(String title, int pages) {
        this.title = title;
        this.pages = pages;
    }
}
rubric: Class declared as public class Book
Both instance variables are private
Correct types: String for title, int for pages
Constructor is public with matching parameters
Constructor initializes both instance variables from parameters

hints.text: Start with public class Book and declare two private instance variables.
The constructor has the same name as the class and takes parameters to initialize the variables (EK 3.4.A.2).

solution_steps.text: Declare the class: public class Book { }
Declare private instance variables: private String title; and private int pages;
Write the constructor: public Book(String title, int pages) and assign parameter values to instance variables.

concepts.title: Methods: How to Write Them
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.5)
  • LO 3.5.A: Define behaviors of an object using methods that work with primitive values.
TermDefinition
void methodA method that performs an action but does not return a value.
Non-void methodA method that returns a value of a specified type.
returnKeyword that returns a value from a method and ends the method's execution.
Accessor methodA non-void method that returns a copy of an instance variable's value (getter).
Mutator methodA method that changes the value of one or more instance variables (setter).
ParameterA variable in a method header that receives a value when the method is called.
ArgumentThe actual value passed to a method when it is called.

void Methods (EK 3.5.A.1)

A void method performs an action but does not return a value (EK 3.5.A.1). The keyword void in the method header indicates no return value.

public void printGreeting() {
    System.out.println("Hello!");
}

Non-void Methods (EK 3.5.A.2 – EK 3.5.A.4)

A non-void method returns a value. The return type in the method header specifies the type of value returned (EK 3.5.A.2). The return statement provides the value and must be compatible with the declared return type (EK 3.5.A.3).

The return keyword immediately ends method execution and returns control to the caller. Any code after a return statement (in the same block) is unreachable and will not execute (EK 3.5.A.4).

public double getArea() {
    return length * width;  // returns a double
    // any code here is unreachable
}

Accessor Methods (EK 3.5.A.5)

An accessor method (getter) is a non-void method that returns a copy of an instance variable’s value (EK 3.5.A.5). It does not modify the object’s state.

public double getGpa() {
    return gpa;  // returns a copy of the value
}

Mutator Methods (EK 3.5.A.6)

A mutator method (setter) changes the value of one or more instance variables (EK 3.5.A.6). Mutator methods are typically void.

public void setGpa(double newGpa) {
    gpa = newGpa;
}

Methods with Parameters (EK 3.5.A.7 – EK 3.5.A.8)

Methods can take parameters to receive data from the caller (EK 3.5.A.7). When a primitive value is passed as an argument, a copy of the value is made. Changes to the parameter inside the method do not affect the original argument (EK 3.5.A.8).

public void deposit(double amount) {
    balance += amount;
    amount = 0;  // does NOT affect the caller's variable
}
Worked Example 1: Complete class with accessors and mutators.
public class Temperature {
    private double degrees;

    public Temperature(double d) {
        degrees = d;
    }

    public double getDegrees() {   // accessor
        return degrees;
    }

    public void setDegrees(double d) {  // mutator
        degrees = d;
    }

    public double toFahrenheit() {  // non-void method
        return degrees * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32;
    }
}
Worked Example 2: Primitive pass-by-value.
public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 10;
    doubleValue(x);
    System.out.println(x);  // prints 10, NOT 20
}

public static void doubleValue(int num) {
    num = num * 2;  // changes local copy only
}

The value of x is copied into num. Changing num does not affect x (EK 3.5.A.8).

AP Trap: Accessor methods return a copy of the value for primitive types. The caller cannot modify the instance variable through the returned value.
AP Trap: Code after a return statement in the same block is unreachable and causes a compile error. The AP exam tests this frequently.
Summary
  • void methods perform actions but return nothing (EK 3.5.A.1).
  • Non-void methods specify a return type and use return (EK 3.5.A.2, EK 3.5.A.3).
  • return exits the method immediately; code after it is unreachable (EK 3.5.A.4).
  • Accessor methods return a copy of an instance variable (EK 3.5.A.5).
  • Mutator methods modify instance variables, typically void (EK 3.5.A.6).
  • Parameters receive data; primitive arguments are copied (EK 3.5.A.7, EK 3.5.A.8).

problem_sets.title: Practice: Methods — How to Write Them

problems.question_html: Which keyword indicates that a method does not return a value?

hints.text: This keyword goes in the method header where the return type would be.
void means 'nothing' — the method returns nothing (EK 3.5.A.1).

solution_steps.text: The void keyword indicates the method does not return a value (EK 3.5.A.1).
A void method performs an action (like printing) instead of computing and returning a result.

problems.question_html:
What is the output of the following code?

public class Demo {
    private int x = 5;

    public int getX() {
        return x;
        x = 10;  // line A
    }
}

choices.text: Compile error: unreachable statement at line A

hints.text: Look at what happens after the return statement.
Code after a return statement in the same block is unreachable (EK 3.5.A.4).

solution_steps.text: The return statement on the line before line A returns control to the caller.
Line A can never execute — it is unreachable. Java detects this at compile time and reports an error (EK 3.5.A.4).

problems.question_html:
What does the following code print?

public static void change(int val) {
    val = val + 5;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int num = 10;
    change(num);
    System.out.println(num);
}

hints.text: num is a primitive (int). What happens when primitives are passed to methods?
Primitive arguments are copied. Changes to the parameter do not affect the argument (EK 3.5.A.8).

solution_steps.text: When change(num) is called, a copy of num (10) is passed to val.
val is changed to 15 inside the method, but num in main remains 10 (EK 3.5.A.8).
The output is 10.

problems.question_html: A non-void method that returns the value of a private instance variable without modifying it is called a(n) _____ method.

hints.text: This type of method 'accesses' data for the caller.
It is also commonly called a getter (EK 3.5.A.5).

solution_steps.text: An accessor method (getter) returns a copy of an instance variable's value (EK 3.5.A.5).
It does not modify the object's state — that is the job of a mutator method.

problems.question_html: A method that changes the value of an instance variable is called a(n) _____ method.

hints.text: This type of method 'mutates' (changes) the object's state.
Also called a setter (EK 3.5.A.6).

solution_steps.text: A mutator method changes the values of instance variables (EK 3.5.A.6).
Mutator methods are typically void since they modify state rather than returning a value.

problems.question_html:
Consider this method:

public int mystery(int a, int b) {
    if (a > b) {
        return a;
    }
    return b;
}

What does mystery(7, 12) return?

hints.text: Trace the code: is 7 > 12?
7 is not greater than 12, so the first return is skipped. The method returns b, which is 12.

solution_steps.text: a = 7, b = 12. Is a > b? 7 > 12 is false, so we skip the if block.
The method reaches return b, which returns 12.
This method returns the larger of the two parameters (the maximum).

problems.question_html: Write a complete class called Counter with a private int count initialized to 0, an accessor method getCount(), and a mutator method increment() that adds 1 to count.
problems.correct_answer:
public class Counter {
    private int count;

    public Counter() {
        count = 0;
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }

    public void increment() {
        count++;
    }
}
rubric: Class declared as public class Counter
Instance variable count is private int
Constructor initializes count to 0
getCount() is public, returns int, returns count
increment() is public void and increases count by 1

hints.text: You need a constructor, one accessor (getCount), and one mutator (increment).
getCount() returns count (EK 3.5.A.5); increment() adds 1 to count (EK 3.5.A.6).

solution_steps.text: Declare private int count as the instance variable.
Write a constructor that sets count = 0.
Write getCount() that returns count (accessor).
Write increment() as void that does count++ (mutator).

concepts.title: Methods: Passing and Returning References of an Object
concepts.content_raw: Methods: Passing and Returning References of an Object
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.6)
  • LO 3.6.A: Define behaviors of an object using methods that use object references.
TermDefinition
Object referenceA variable that stores the memory address of an object, not the object itself.
AliasingWhen two or more reference variables point to the same object in memory.
Pass by valueJava always copies the value of an argument; for references, the reference (address) is copied.
nullA special value meaning a reference does not point to any object.

Passing Object References (EK 3.6.A.1)

When an object reference is passed as an argument, a copy of the reference is made — not a copy of the object itself (EK 3.6.A.1). Both the argument and the parameter now point to the same object in memory. This means the method can alter the state of a mutable object through the reference.

public void addStudent(ArrayList<String> roster, String name) {
    roster.add(name);  // modifies the SAME ArrayList the caller has
}

Compare this to primitives (EK 3.5.A.8): for primitives, changes to the parameter do not affect the argument. For object references, the parameter and argument both refer to the same object, so changes to the object are visible to the caller.

Returning Object References (EK 3.6.A.2)

When a method returns an object reference, it returns the reference itself, not a copy of the object (EK 3.6.A.2). The caller receives a reference to the exact same object in memory.

public String getName() {
    return name;  // returns a reference to the same String object
}

Private Data Access Rules (EK 3.6.A.3)

A method cannot access the private data of an object passed as a parameter unless the parameter’s type is the same class as the enclosing class (EK 3.6.A.3). For example, a method in Dog can access the private fields of another Dog object, but not the private fields of a Cat object.

public class Dog {
    private String name;

    public boolean sameName(Dog other) {
        return name.equals(other.name);  // OK: same class
    }
}
Worked Example 1: Object reference aliasing.
public class Demo {
    public static void changeName(Dog d) {
        d.setName("Buddy");  // modifies the original Dog
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog myDog = new Dog("Rex");
        changeName(myDog);
        System.out.println(myDog.getName()); // prints "Buddy"
    }
}

The reference myDog is copied to parameter d. Both point to the same Dog object, so d.setName("Buddy") changes the original Dog (EK 3.6.A.1).

Worked Example 2: Returning a reference.
public class Classroom {
    private ArrayList<String> students;

    public ArrayList<String> getStudents() {
        return students;  // returns reference, not a copy!
    }
}

The caller receives a reference to the actual students list. If the caller modifies the returned list, the Classroom object’s state changes too (EK 3.6.A.2).

AP Trap: Passing an object reference copies the reference, not the object. Both the caller and the method see the same object. This is different from primitives, where changes to the parameter do not affect the argument.
AP Trap: A method in class X cannot access private fields of a parameter of type Y (where Y is a different class). But a method in class X can access private fields of a parameter of type X (same class).
Summary
  • Object reference arguments copy the reference, not the object (EK 3.6.A.1).
  • Methods can modify a mutable object through its copied reference (EK 3.6.A.1).
  • Returning a reference returns the reference, not a copy of the object (EK 3.6.A.2).
  • Private data of a parameter object is accessible only if the parameter's type is the same class (EK 3.6.A.3).
  • Primitives are copied by value; object references are also copied, but the copy points to the same object.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Methods — Passing and Returning References

problems.question_html: When an object reference is passed to a method, what is actually copied?

choices.text: The reference (memory address) to the object
A deep copy of the object

hints.text: Java always passes by value, but for objects the value IS the reference.
A copy of the reference is made, so both point to the same object (EK 3.6.A.1).

solution_steps.text: Java passes a copy of the reference (memory address), not the object itself (EK 3.6.A.1).
Both the argument and parameter point to the same object, so changes to the object are visible to the caller.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following code:

public static void addItem(ArrayList<String> list) {
    list.add("New");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    ArrayList<String> items = new ArrayList<String>();
    items.add("Old");
    addItem(items);
    System.out.println(items.size());
}

What does this code print?

hints.text: The ArrayList reference is copied, but both references point to the same list.
addItem modifies the same ArrayList that items points to (EK 3.6.A.1).

solution_steps.text: items starts with one element ("Old"). The reference to items is copied to the parameter list.
list.add("New") modifies the same ArrayList. After addItem returns, items has 2 elements.
items.size() returns 2.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following code:

public class Point {
    private int x;
    private int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    public boolean sameLocation(Point other) {
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;
    }
}

Does the sameLocation method compile? Why or why not?

choices.text: No, because other.x and other.y are private
Yes, because both objects are of type Point (same class)
No, because you must use getters to access x and y
Yes, because all instance variables are always accessible

hints.text: The parameter other is of type Point — the same class where the method is defined.
A method can access private fields of another object if that object's type is the same class (EK 3.6.A.3).

solution_steps.text: The parameter other is of type Point, and sameLocation is defined in class Point.
A method can access private data of a parameter when the parameter's type matches the enclosing class (EK 3.6.A.3).
So other.x and other.y are legal — the code compiles and works correctly.

problems.question_html: When a non-void method returns an object, it returns a copy of the _____.

hints.text: The method does not copy the entire object.
The return expression evaluates to a reference, and that reference is returned (EK 3.6.A.2).

solution_steps.text: When returning an object, the reference is returned — not a copy of the object itself (EK 3.6.A.2).
The caller receives a reference to the exact same object in memory.

problems.question_html: A method in class A receives a parameter of type B. Can the method access B's private instance variables directly?

hints.text: Think about which class has access to private fields.
Private data is only accessible within the same class (EK 3.6.A.3).

solution_steps.text: A method cannot access private data of a parameter unless the parameter's type is the same as the enclosing class (EK 3.6.A.3).
Class A cannot access class B's private fields. You must use B's public methods.

problems.question_html: Write a method swap inside a class Pair that has two private instance variables first and second (both int). The method should swap their values. Include the full class.
problems.correct_answer:
public class Pair {
    private int first;
    private int second;

    public Pair(int f, int s) {
        first = f;
        second = s;
    }

    public void swap() {
        int temp = first;
        first = second;
        second = temp;
    }

    public int getFirst() { return first; }
    public int getSecond() { return second; }
}
rubric: Class is public class Pair with private int first and int second
Constructor initializes both instance variables
swap() is a void method that correctly swaps first and second using a temporary variable
Accessor methods provided for first and second

hints.text: To swap two values, you need a temporary variable to hold one value.
int temp = first; first = second; second = temp;

solution_steps.text: Declare private int first and private int second.
Write a constructor that initializes both from parameters.
In swap(), use a temp variable: int temp = first; first = second; second = temp;
Add accessor methods getFirst() and getSecond() for completeness.

concepts.title: Class Variables and Methods
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.7)
  • LO 3.7.A: Define class methods.
  • LO 3.7.B: Declare class variables.
TermDefinition
static methodA method that belongs to the class, not to any particular object instance.
static variableA variable shared by all instances of a class; declared with the static keyword.
finalA keyword that makes a variable’s value unchangeable after initialization.
Class methodAnother name for a static method; called using the class name.
Class variableAnother name for a static variable; one copy shared by all objects.

Class (Static) Methods (EK 3.7.A.1 – EK 3.7.A.2)

Class methods (static methods) belong to the class itself, not to any particular object (LO 3.7.A). They are declared with the static keyword.

Key rule: a static method cannot access instance variables directly, because there is no specific object (EK 3.7.A.1). To use instance data, the method must receive an object as a parameter.

A static method can access class (static) variables and call other static methods (EK 3.7.A.2).

public class MathHelper {
    public static int square(int n) {
        return n * n;  // no instance variables needed
    }
}

// Called with class name:
int result = MathHelper.square(5);  // 25

Class (Static) Variables (EK 3.7.B.1 – EK 3.7.B.3)

Class variables are declared with the static keyword and are shared by all instances of the class (EK 3.7.B.1). There is only one copy in memory, no matter how many objects are created.

public class variables are accessed using the class name and the dot operator (EK 3.7.B.2): ClassName.variableName.

A variable declared final cannot be modified after initialization (EK 3.7.B.3). Constants are typically public static final.

public class Dog {
    private static int dogCount = 0;      // class variable
    public static final String SPECIES = "Canis lupus";  // constant
    private String name;

    public Dog(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        dogCount++;  // shared counter increments
    }

    public static int getDogCount() {  // class method
        return dogCount;
    }
}
Worked Example 1: Static vs. instance access.
public class Counter {
    private static int total = 0;
    private int id;

    public Counter() {
        total++;
        id = total;
    }

    public static int getTotal() {
        return total;  // OK: static method accessing static variable
        // return id;  // ERROR: cannot access instance variable
    }

    public int getId() {
        return id;  // OK: instance method can access both
    }
}

Counter c1 = new Counter();  // total=1, c1.id=1
Counter c2 = new Counter();  // total=2, c2.id=2
System.out.println(Counter.getTotal());  // 2
Worked Example 2: Using final.
public class Circle {
    public static final double PI = 3.14159265;

    public static double area(double radius) {
        return PI * radius * radius;
    }
}

double a = Circle.area(5.0);
System.out.println(Circle.PI);  // 3.14159265

PI is public static final: accessible via class name and cannot be modified.

AP Trap: A static method cannot use this or access instance variables without an object reference. This is a very common AP exam question.
AP Trap: A final variable can be assigned once. Attempting to change its value causes a compile error.
Summary
  • Static methods belong to the class and cannot access instance variables without a parameter (EK 3.7.A.1).
  • Static methods can access static variables and call other static methods (EK 3.7.A.2).
  • Static variables are shared by all instances; use static keyword (EK 3.7.B.1).
  • Public static variables are accessed via ClassName.varName (EK 3.7.B.2).
  • final prevents modification after initialization (EK 3.7.B.3).
  • Constants are typically public static final.

problems.question_html: Which keyword makes a variable or method belong to the class rather than to a specific object?

hints.text: This keyword means 'belonging to the class, not to an instance.'
The static keyword declares class-level variables and methods (EK 3.7.B.1).

solution_steps.text: The static keyword makes a variable or method belong to the class itself (EK 3.7.B.1).
Static members are shared by all instances and can be accessed with the class name.

problems.question_html: Can a static method call another static method in the same class?

choices.text: No, static methods cannot call any other methods
Yes, static methods can call other static methods and access static variables
Only if the other method is also public
Only if an object is created first

hints.text: Static methods operate at the class level.
Static methods can access class-level members: other static methods and static variables (EK 3.7.A.2).

solution_steps.text: Static methods can call other static methods and access static variables in the same class (EK 3.7.A.2).
They cannot access instance variables or instance methods without an object reference (EK 3.7.A.1).

problems.question_html: What happens if you try to access an instance variable from a static method (without an object reference)?

choices.text: It returns the default value of the variable

hints.text: A static method does not have a specific object to refer to.
Static methods cannot access instance variables directly (EK 3.7.A.1). This is caught at compile time.

solution_steps.text: A static method cannot access instance variables because it has no 'this' object (EK 3.7.A.1).
The Java compiler detects this and reports a compile error.

problems.question_html: A variable declared with the _____ keyword cannot be changed after initialization.

hints.text: This keyword means 'this is the last value — it cannot change.'
The _____ keyword prevents modification (EK 3.7.B.3).

solution_steps.text: The final keyword makes a variable's value permanent — it cannot be reassigned (EK 3.7.B.3).
Constants like Math.PI are declared public static final.

problems.question_html: Public static variables are accessed using the _____ name and the dot operator.

hints.text: Static members belong to the class, not to objects.
ClassName.variableName is the syntax (EK 3.7.B.2).

solution_steps.text: Public static variables are accessed using the class name and dot: ClassName.varName (EK 3.7.B.2).
Example: Math.PI uses the class name Math to access the static final variable PI.

problems.question_html:
Consider the following class:

public class Tracker {
    private static int count = 0;

    public Tracker() {
        count++;
    }

    public static int getCount() {
        return count;
    }
}

Tracker t1 = new Tracker();
Tracker t2 = new Tracker();
Tracker t3 = new Tracker();
System.out.println(Tracker.getCount());

What is printed?

hints.text: count is static — shared across all instances. Each constructor call increments it.
Three Tracker objects are created, so count is incremented three times.

solution_steps.text: count starts at 0. Each new Tracker() increments count by 1.
After 3 Tracker objects, count = 3. Tracker.getCount() returns 3.

problems.question_html: Write a class IDGenerator with a private static variable nextId starting at 1000, a private instance variable id, and a constructor that assigns nextId to id and then increments nextId. Include a getId() accessor and a static getNextId() method.
problems.correct_answer:
public class IDGenerator {
    private static int nextId = 1000;
    private int id;

    public IDGenerator() {
        id = nextId;
        nextId++;
    }

    public int getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public static int getNextId() {
        return nextId;
    }
}
rubric: private static int nextId initialized to 1000
private int id (instance variable)
Constructor assigns nextId to id and increments nextId
getId() is an instance method returning id
getNextId() is a static method returning nextId

hints.text: nextId is shared (static), id is unique per object (instance).
In the constructor: id = nextId; nextId++;

solution_steps.text: Declare private static int nextId = 1000 (shared counter).
Declare private int id (unique per object).
Constructor: id = nextId; nextId++; — each object gets the current ID, then the counter advances.
getId() returns the instance's id; getNextId() is static and returns the class's nextId.

concepts.title: Scope and Access
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.8)
  • LO 3.8.A: Explain where variables can be used in program code.
TermDefinition
ScopeThe region of code where a variable can be accessed.
Local variableA variable declared inside a method body or block; only accessible within that block.
ParameterA local variable declared in a method header that receives an argument value.
Instance variableDeclared in the class body (outside any method); accessible throughout the class.
ShadowingWhen a local variable or parameter has the same name as an instance variable, hiding it within that scope.

Local Variables and Scope (EK 3.8.A.1)

Local variables are declared inside method bodies, constructor bodies, or other blocks like loops and if-statements (EK 3.8.A.1). A local variable can only be accessed within the block where it is declared. Once the block ends, the variable is out of scope and no longer exists.

Parameters are local variables declared in method or constructor headers (EK 3.8.A.1). They have the same scope as the method body.

public class Demo {
    private int x = 10;  // instance variable — accessible everywhere in class

    public void example(int y) {  // y is a parameter (local)
        int z = 5;  // z is a local variable
        // x, y, and z are all accessible here
    }
    // y and z are NOT accessible here
}

Variable Shadowing (EK 3.8.A.2)

If a local variable or parameter has the same name as an instance variable, the local variable takes precedence within the method (EK 3.8.A.2). This is called shadowing. The instance variable is hidden, and the name refers to the local variable.

public class Shadow {
    private int value = 100;

    public void setValue(int value) {  // parameter shadows instance variable
        // 'value' here refers to the PARAMETER, not the instance variable
        System.out.println(value);  // prints the parameter value
    }
}

To access the instance variable when it is shadowed, use the this keyword (covered in Topic 3.9).

Worked Example 1: Scope of local variables.
public void demo() {
    int a = 1;
    if (a > 0) {
        int b = 2;
        System.out.println(a + b);  // OK: a and b in scope
    }
    // System.out.println(b);  // ERROR: b is out of scope
    System.out.println(a);  // OK: a is still in scope
}

b is declared inside the if-block, so it only exists within that block. Trying to use b outside causes a compile error.

Worked Example 2: Shadowing in action.
public class Box {
    private int size = 10;

    public void setSize(int size) {
        // 'size' refers to the parameter, not the instance variable
        System.out.println(size);  // prints the parameter
    }

    public int getSize() {
        return size;  // no shadowing — refers to instance variable
    }
}

Box b = new Box();
b.setSize(25);  // prints 25
System.out.println(b.getSize());  // prints 10 (instance variable unchanged!)

In setSize, the parameter size shadows the instance variable. The assignment size = 25 does not change the instance variable — you would need this.size = size; (Topic 3.9).

AP Trap: When a parameter has the same name as an instance variable, the parameter takes precedence. If you write size = size;, you are assigning the parameter to itself — the instance variable is unchanged.
AP Trap: A variable declared inside a loop or if-block is only accessible within that block. Using it outside causes a compile error.
Summary
  • Local variables are declared in method bodies/blocks and only accessible within that block (EK 3.8.A.1).
  • Parameters are local variables declared in method headers (EK 3.8.A.1).
  • Instance variables are accessible throughout the class.
  • When a local variable has the same name as an instance variable, the local variable takes precedence (EK 3.8.A.2).
  • Use this to access the instance variable when shadowed (Topic 3.9).

problems.question_html:
What is printed by the following code?

public class Test {
    private int x = 5;

    public void show(int x) {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Test t = new Test();
t.show(20);

hints.text: The parameter x shadows the instance variable x.
When a local variable has the same name as an instance variable, the local takes precedence (EK 3.8.A.2).

solution_steps.text: The parameter x (value 20) shadows the instance variable x (value 5).
Inside show(), x refers to the parameter, so it prints 20 (EK 3.8.A.2).

problems.question_html:
What happens when you try to compile this code?

public void example() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        int sum = 0;
    }
    System.out.println(sum);
}

choices.text: Compile error: sum is out of scope

hints.text: Where is sum declared? What is its scope?
sum is declared inside the for loop body, so it is out of scope outside the loop (EK 3.8.A.1).

solution_steps.text: sum is declared inside the for loop block, so its scope is limited to that block (EK 3.8.A.1).
Accessing sum outside the loop causes a compile error because it is out of scope.

problems.question_html: A variable declared inside a method body can only be accessed within that method. This variable is called a _____ variable.

hints.text: It is 'local' to the method where it is declared.
Local variables are declared in headers or bodies and accessible only in their block (EK 3.8.A.1).

solution_steps.text: A local variable is declared inside a method body or block (EK 3.8.A.1).
It can only be accessed within the block where it is declared. Parameters are also local variables.

problems.question_html: When a local variable or parameter has the same name as an instance variable, the _____ variable takes precedence within the method.

hints.text: The variable closer to the current scope wins.
A local variable/parameter shadows the instance variable (EK 3.8.A.2).

solution_steps.text: When names conflict, the local variable (or parameter) takes precedence within the method (EK 3.8.A.2).
The instance variable is 'shadowed' and can only be accessed using this.variableName.

problems.question_html:
Consider this code:

public class Widget {
    private int count = 0;

    public void add(int count) {
        count = count + 1;
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }
}

Widget w = new Widget();
w.add(5);
System.out.println(w.getCount());

What is printed?

hints.text: In the add method, which 'count' is being modified?
The parameter count shadows the instance variable count. count = count + 1 modifies the parameter only (EK 3.8.A.2).

solution_steps.text: In add(), the parameter count shadows the instance variable count.
count = count + 1 modifies the parameter (6), not the instance variable (still 0).
getCount() returns the instance variable, which is still 0.

problems.question_html: Write a method findMax that takes an array of integers as a parameter and returns the maximum value. Use proper local variable scope.
problems.correct_answer:
public static int findMax(int[] arr) {
    int max = arr[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
        if (arr[i] > max) {
            max = arr[i];
        }
    }
    return max;
}
rubric: Method header is correct: returns int, takes int[] parameter
Local variable max initialized to first element
Loop iterates through the array comparing values
Returns the maximum value found

hints.text: Start by assuming the first element is the max, then compare each element.
Declare max as a local variable initialized to arr[0], then loop and update as needed.

solution_steps.text: Declare local variable max = arr[0] to hold the current maximum.
Loop from index 1 to arr.length - 1, updating max whenever a larger value is found.
Return max after the loop completes.

concepts.title: this Keyword
concepts.content_html:
Learning Objectives (CED 3.9)
  • LO 3.9.A: Create self-referencing expressions using the keyword this.
TermDefinition
thisA keyword that holds a reference to the current object within an instance method or constructor.
Self-referenceAn object referring to itself using this.
DisambiguationUsing this to distinguish an instance variable from a local variable with the same name.
Instance methodA non-static method that belongs to a specific object and has access to this.

The this Keyword (EK 3.9.A.1)

The keyword this holds a reference to the current object — the object on which the method or constructor is being called (EK 3.9.A.1). It is used inside instance methods and constructors to refer to the object itself.

The most common use of this is to disambiguate when a parameter or local variable has the same name as an instance variable:

public class Dog {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Dog(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;  // this.name = instance variable, name = parameter
        this.age = age;
    }
}

Without this, the parameter name shadows the instance variable, and name = name would just assign the parameter to itself (doing nothing useful).

Passing this as an Argument (EK 3.9.A.2)

this can be passed as an argument to another method, allowing the current object to be sent to another method or object (EK 3.9.A.2).

public class Player {
    private String name;

    public Player(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public void joinTeam(Team team) {
        team.addPlayer(this);  // passes the current Player object
    }
}

Class Methods and this (EK 3.9.A.3)

Class (static) methods do not have this (EK 3.9.A.3). Since static methods belong to the class and not to any object, there is no “current object” to reference. Using this in a static method causes a compile error.

Worked Example 1: Using this in a constructor.
public class Rectangle {
    private double length;
    private double width;

    public Rectangle(double length, double width) {
        this.length = length;  // instance var = parameter
        this.width = width;
    }

    public double getArea() {
        return this.length * this.width;  // 'this' optional here
    }
}

In the constructor, this.length refers to the instance variable, while length alone refers to the parameter. In getArea(), this is optional because there is no shadowing.

Worked Example 2: Passing this as an argument.
public class Student {
    private String name;

    public Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public void enroll(Course course) {
        course.addStudent(this);  // pass this Student to the Course
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }
}

this passes the current Student object to course.addStudent(), so the course can store a reference to the student (EK 3.9.A.2).

Worked Example 3: this in a mutator method.
public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double balance) {
        this.balance = balance;
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        this.balance += amount;  // 'this' optional (no shadowing)
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return this.balance;
    }
}
AP Trap: Using this in a static method causes a compile error. Static methods have no current object, so this does not exist (EK 3.9.A.3).
AP Trap: this.name = name is NOT the same as name = name. Without this, the parameter shadows the instance variable and the assignment does nothing useful.
Summary
  • this is a reference to the current object in an instance method or constructor (EK 3.9.A.1).
  • Use this.varName to distinguish an instance variable from a same-named parameter.
  • this can be passed as an argument to another method (EK 3.9.A.2).
  • Static methods do not have this (EK 3.9.A.3).
  • this is optional when there is no naming conflict.

problems.question_html: What does the keyword this refer to?

choices.text: The current object on which the method is called

hints.text: 'this' is a self-reference to the object executing the method.
this holds a reference to the current object (EK 3.9.A.1).

solution_steps.text: The keyword this refers to the current object — the object on which the method or constructor is called (EK 3.9.A.1).
It is used to access instance variables and methods of the current object.

problems.question_html:
What is printed by the following code?

public class Item {
    private int value;

    public Item(int value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public int getValue() {
        return value;
    }
}

Item item = new Item(42);
System.out.println(item.getValue());

hints.text: In the constructor, this.value = value assigns the parameter to the instance variable.
this.value refers to the instance variable; value (without this) refers to the parameter (EK 3.9.A.1).

solution_steps.text: The constructor receives value = 42. this.value = value assigns 42 to the instance variable.
getValue() returns the instance variable value, which is 42.

problems.question_html:
In the following code, does this in the register method compile?

public class Sensor {
    private String id;

    public Sensor(String id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public static void register(Hub hub) {
        hub.add(this);  // line A
    }
}

choices.text: Yes, this always works in any method
No, because register is static and static methods cannot use this
Yes, because hub.add() accepts any object
No, because Hub is a different class

hints.text: Look at the method signature — is it static or instance?
register is static. Static methods do not have this (EK 3.9.A.3).

solution_steps.text: The register method is declared static, so it does not belong to any specific object.
Static methods do not have a this reference (EK 3.9.A.3). Using this in a static method causes a compile error.

problems.question_html:
this can be used in a static method.

True or false?

hints.text: Static methods belong to the class, not to any specific object.
Class methods do not have this (EK 3.9.A.3).

solution_steps.text: False. Static (class) methods do not have a this reference because they do not belong to any specific object (EK 3.9.A.3).
Using this in a static method causes a compile error.

problems.question_html: this can be passed as a(n) _____ to another method.

hints.text: When you call a method and pass this, you are passing the current object.
this can be passed as an argument to send the current object to another method (EK 3.9.A.2).

solution_steps.text: this can be passed as an argument to a method that expects an object of the current class's type (EK 3.9.A.2).
This allows the current object to register itself with another object, for example.

problems.question_html:
What is printed by the following code?

public class Mystery {
    private int x;

    public Mystery(int x) {
        x = x;  // note: no 'this' keyword
    }

    public int getX() {
        return x;
    }
}

Mystery m = new Mystery(99);
System.out.println(m.getX());

hints.text: Look carefully at the constructor: x = x (without this).
The parameter x shadows the instance variable x. x = x assigns the parameter to itself (EK 3.8.A.2). The instance variable keeps its default value of 0.

solution_steps.text: In the constructor, x = x assigns the parameter to itself because the parameter shadows the instance variable.
The instance variable x is never assigned, so it retains its default value of 0 (EK 3.4.A.5).
getX() returns 0. To fix this, use this.x = x.

problems.question_html: Write a complete class called Person with a private String name and a private int age. Write a constructor that uses this to disambiguate parameters with the same names as the instance variables. Include accessor methods for both fields.
problems.correct_answer:
public class Person {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }
}
rubric: Class declared as public class Person
Private instance variables name (String) and age (int)
Constructor uses this.name = name and this.age = age for disambiguation
getName() returns name, getAge() returns age

hints.text: The constructor parameters should have the same names as the instance variables.
Use this.name = name; and this.age = age; in the constructor (EK 3.9.A.1).

solution_steps.text: Declare private String name and private int age as instance variables.
Constructor: public Person(String name, int age) with this.name = name; this.age = age;
Add accessor methods: getName() returns name, getAge() returns age.
